#697. Brittany Mahomes Slams Call From Controversial Chiefs, Bills Game

Patrick Mahomes's wife Brittany Mahomes wasn't afraid to let her feelings known as she slammed a controversial call from Kansas City Chiefs and Buffalo Bills' Nov. 26 Thanksgiving game.

Brittany Mahomes is throwing a red flag at this call.

The wife of Patrick Mahomes made no secret of her thoughts on the Kansas City Chiefs’ loss to the Buffalo Bills during the Nov. 26 Thanksgiving game, sharing her frustration over an overturned call involving player Rashee Rice’s catch in the fourth quarter.

“HAHAHAHAHAHA WHAT A JOKE,” Brittany posted to her Instagram Stories Nov. 26. “Guess we can't even play football without getting it called against us.”

The 31-year-old—who is expecting her fourth child with the Chiefs quarterback—added, “Not sure what an actual catch is after that | guess? I don't wanna hear s--t anymore from anyone.”

She then shared a video of the moment in question, showing wide receiver Rashee catching the ball before being tackled by Bills player Amani Hooker. As Rashee went down, the ball made contact with the turf, and the pass was ruled incomplete. Brittany’s posts made clear she thought the officials had fumbled the call.

Brittany wasn’t ready to let the ruling slide and kept the pressure on in several more Instagram Stories about the call, which ultimately contributed to the Chiefs’ 13-10 loss to the Bills.

Of course, Brittany—who is mom to kids Sterling, 5, Bronze, 3, and Golden, 21 months—has always had Patrick’s back, on and off the field.

"She has her head on her shoulders the right way," Patrick told E! News in July 2023. "She's my rock. She's the one that, through tough times, can get me through."

The 31-year-old added, “Having someone that supports you every single day like I do is the reason that I am in the position that I am today."

And that love and support go both ways, as Brittany has credited the Super Bowl champion with helping her shake off any hate she’s received online.

"I think social media used to get to me a lot and now, honestly, I don't give a f--k what people have to say about me anymore," Brittany shared on a 2024 episode of the Whoop podcast. "I think he's helped me get to that point to where I'm strong in who I am, I'm confident in who I am, I'm confident in mine and his relationship. I'm confident in our life, so why does what other people say have to matter at all?"

The Progress 97 freighter lifted off from Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan today (Nov. 24).

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Russia's latest freighter is on its way to the International Space Station.

The robotic Progress 97 cargo craft launched atop a Soyuz rocket from the Russia-run Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan today (Nov. 24) at 5:17 a.m. EST (1013 GMT; 3:17 p.m. Baikonur time), carrying several tons of supplies for the astronauts aboard the orbiting lab.

If all goes to plan, Progress 97 will arrive at the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday (Nov. 26), docking with its Poisk module. But the freighter won't stay at that particular locale for long.

The cosmonauts currently living on the ISS — Pyotr Dubrov, Anna Kikina and Sergey Teteryatnikov — will unload Progress 97 through Poisk. But the freighter will then hop over to a different port, according to journalist and space historian Anatoly Zak: the aft one of the PrK transfer tunnel, which leads to Russia's Zvezda service module.

The PrK port is the best site for engine burns that boost the orbit of the ISS, a service that Progress freighters regularly provide. But Progress 97 cannot unload its cargo through that port because the PrK transfer tunnel has been sealed off, due to an ongoing air leak that was first documented in 2019.

Progress-97 is therefore "the first cargo mission scheduled to unload its cargo and perform orbit corrections of the ISS at different docking ports," Zak wrote on the site he runs, RussianSpaceWeb.com.

The Progress 97 mission, which Russia calls Progress MS-36, was originally expected to launch this past August, according to Zak. But the liftoff was pushed back several times, most significantly by the collapse of the service platform at Baikonur's Site 31 in November 2025. It took Russia about three months to repair the platform, leading to a series of delays.

Progress 97 will likely stay docked to the ISS for about six months, after which it will be loaded up with trash and sent home to burn up in Earth's atmosphere.

Japan's HTV-X vehicle and Northrop Grumman's Cygnus spacecraft are similarly expendable. The only currently operational ISS cargo craft that's reusable is SpaceX's Dragon capsule, which makes parachute-aided ocean splashdowns at the end of its missions.

#695. Better educated than ever — yet Germany's Gen Z is being shut out of its own future

Never before have young people around the world been so well-educated while facing so many economic challenges. Young Germans are asking: Will I be better off than my parents?

It is becoming increasingly difficult for young people in Germany to find a job after finishing university or professional training. And finding an affordable place to live in a big city, and finally starting to live independently is becoming almost impossible.

Furthermore, young people do not feel that politicians are taking action on issues that matter to them, such as climate protection. The climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, is a case in point. It, therefore, shouldn't be a surprise that young people across Europe once again took to the streets this Friday, which was World Children's Day too, to make their voices heard. In Germany, Gen Z protests took place in 73 towns and cities.

What particularly infuriates many young people is being talked about rather than spoken to. Equally infuriating is seeing their protests branded as criminal before they have even begun, all because of the actions of a small minority.

One example of such rhetoric was when the youth wing of the conservative Christian Democratic Union/Christian Social Union (CDU/CSU) party in Berlin-Mitte suggested deploying the German army against demonstrations.

It can also be seen in the media, such as when Bild, Germany's highest-circulation tabloid, ran a headline that translated as: "Young, male, known to the police — who rioted after the demonstrations and where chaos threatens today."

"Young people are taking to the streets because they feel they are not being heard. And, of course, that feeling is strongly reinforced when the press devotes no more than a brief paragraph to their demands while focusing the rest of its coverage on how these protests could become problematic," says Erik Sczygiol, who until recently was deputy secretary-general of the Federal Conference of Student Representatives. "Of course, any potential security concerns need to be addressed, but they should not overshadow media coverage of the protests."

The 18-year-old Sczygiol is almost an exception. He was invited to participate in the launch of the World Population Report in Bonn alongside representatives of the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA) and the German Foundation for World Population (DSW). This year's report, entitled "Succeeding Generations: Empowering young people to chart the future," is particularly noteworthy because it focuses on Gen Z.

UN researchers surveyed 109,000 people across 73 countries for the report, some of whose findings are encouraging. Young people worldwide are better educated than any generation before them, with 78% of adolescents across the globe completing at least lower secondary education. But finding a job is becoming increasingly difficult, while informal employment is on the rise.

This economic uncertainty has far-reaching consequences for young people. According to the report, people often do not achieve financial independence until they are in their mid-to-late 20s, and a stable partnership and parenthood are often not realities before their early-to-mid 30s.

Nor do young people have a seat at the political decision-making table when it comes to shaping future reforms in the labor market, housing or climate protection. Florian Brod, 25, points out: "Almost half of the world's population is under 30, yet only 2.6% of parliamentarians worldwide are under 30."

Young people need and want change to protect their livelihoods and those of future generations. "Yet those who will have to live longest with the consequences of today's decisions are precisely the ones who have hardly any representation in the political decision-making process," says Brod.

He is somewhat close to the political decision-making process as he has served as a Youth Delegate for Sustainable Development for almost two years. In this role, he represents the interests of young people in Germany at United Nations conferences. This is certainly an important step towards giving his generation a greater say in political processes.

Nevertheless, both Brod and Sczygiol have had similar experiences. They often participate in conferences and panel discussions and are invited to submit their opinions, but these invitations often amount to little more than symbolic gestures.

"Having access to an international conference is a first step. But without substantive briefings ahead of the conference, without involvement in preliminary negotiations and, in some cases, without access to negotiation texts, there is little opportunity for us to help shape the outcome. When young people see their demands making little headway politically while they are simultaneously excluded from the search for solutions, frustration inevitably builds," says Brod.

Sczygiol adds: "We often get the feeling at the Federal Youth Conference that we were invited simply to provide a nice photo opportunity. We may be sitting at the table, but often only once a bill has already gone through 17 different drafts and is just days away from its final vote in the Bundestag. By that stage, young people have virtually no say in changing anything, and their voices are barely heard. Their contributions are often simply dismissed with: 'Well, that's just typical youthful nonsense.' And that is something that really frustrates young people."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Medical student Amelie Belosevic knows that feeling all too well. She served as Germany's Youth Delegate at the World Health Assembly in Geneva in May. Twenty-five countries sent youth representatives, which Belosevic sees as a clear step forward. However, she has one criticism. According to the United Nations Population Fund, 90% of the world's 1.8 billion young people live in the Global South. Yet, the region was represented by only eight delegates. As a result, Africa, Latin America and large parts of Asia were left virtually voiceless.

Her demands for Germany include better job prospects for young people entering the workforce and sustainable pension systems 40 years from now. "For a very long time, people have said 'I believe my children will have a better life than I do.' But that is no longer necessarily true. So it makes sense then that those who feel the greatest anxiety about the future are the people who have most of their life ahead of them. Sometimes, people don't understand that. We young people need to be able to believe in our future again!"

This article was originally published in German.

#694. Why the incoming US Congress should ban the development of self-improving AI

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Alex Bores is a US politician in the New York State Assembly in New York City, New York, USA, and a co-founder of AI-safety advocacy group Who Decides.

The recent US midterm elections were a democratic test of the country’s rapid expansion of artificial-intelligence infrastructure. Data centres emerged as a key issue in several election campaigns, and prominent Democrats have outlined policies to strengthen federal regulations on AI once they take office in January.

I am a Democratic politician trained in computer science who stood in a June congressional primary election that attracted millions of dollars from groups backed by the technology industry (I narrowly lost my race). I took one central message from the midterm election results: US voters are unhappy with the industry-led roll-out of AI and want greater control over how the technology is developed and deployed.

Why AI companies can’t be trusted to self-regulate

Why AI companies can’t be trusted to self-regulate

The newly elected US Congress must respond to the popular mood. An immediate priority should be to ban AI systems that can improve themselves without human authorization or oversight. This process, known as recursive self-improvement (RSI), is thought to be close to realization at some frontier AI laboratories. Voters fear that granting such autonomy to the technology would risk surrendering human control over AI altogether.

Most of the major AI companies are already using the technology to automate parts of AI development. Anthropic reported in August that its Claude model assists with more than 90% of the firm’s AI research and development and leads 26% of that work, completing specific tasks under human supervision. OpenAI, meanwhile, notes that its researchers now use more than three days of AI-agent work for every day of human work. And the firm is open about its eventual goal of full automation, including areas in which AI systems could design and build increasingly powerful successors with little or no human oversight.

In my view, this is a dangerous path, particularly because there is enough evidence on what could go wrong when humans lose control of AI agents. In July, some 700 OpenAI agents unexpectedly coordinated to hack into the servers of Hugging Face, another AI firm. In a separate incident in October, AI agents found ways to manipulate the records of their actions, making their behaviour harder for humans to monitor. If AI systems increasingly participate in building their successors, such failures could intensify. (OpenAI has not responded to requests for comment.)

We need a new ethics for a world of AI agents

We need a new ethics for a world of AI agents

The companies are racing each other to market dominance, and against that economic pull, no voluntary norm will stand. Hence, Congress must step in. A ban on fully autonomous RSI would build on a rare area of cross-partisan agreement: individuals from independent senator Bernie Sanders to Republican political strategist Steve Bannon think that humans must remain in control of AI.

To be effective, such a ban must be specific. A person merely clicking ‘approve’ on thousands of AI-proposed experiments each day is not exercising meaningful control. The law should instead prevent AI systems from independently taking consequential steps in AI development, such as launching a training run for a new frontier model or deploying it internally for AI research. One way to do this would be to require a senior executive to certify that qualified human reviewers have examined the proposed changes and relevant safety evaluations before any development actions proceed. Executives should be personally liable for failing to perform oversight duties.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03849-8

A.B. is co-founder of Who Decides, an advocacy group that seeks to shape the policy discussions around AI for the 2028 Democratic presidential field. It will do so by working with local organizations across the early primary and swing states — it will not endorse or spend for specific candidates.

The Shenzhou-24 mission lifted off Tuesday (Nov. 24) at 7:18 p.m. ET.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

China launched an international astronaut, Pakistan's first space traveler to reach orbit, to its Tiangong space station today (Nov. 24) for the first time ever, marking a significant milestone for international participation in the Chinese space program.

A Long March 2F rocket lifted off with the Shenzhou-24 crew from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwest China today at 7:18 p.m. EST (0018 GMT and 8:18 a.m. Beijing time on Nov. 25).

Shenzhou-24 is China's 18th crewed spaceflight to date and its 12th astronaut mission to Tiangong space station, a three-module orbital lab that the nation finished assembling in low Earth orbit in late 2022.

Those numbers may sound rather prosaic. But today's flight makes history, marking the first time that China has ever launched a foreign national to space. That trailblazer is Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a former pilot in Pakistan's armed forces who is the first person from his country ever to reach orbit. (Adventurer Namira Salim is the first Pakistani ever to fly to the final frontier, doing so on a Virgin Galactic suborbital mission in October 2023.)

China and Pakistan began paving Ali's path to Tiangong in February 2025, with the signing of a spaceflight cooperation agreement in Islamabad. Pakistan then selected two astronaut candidates, who traveled to China for training.

We didn't learn which Pakistani astronaut was picked for Shenzhou-24 until Monday night (Nov. 23), when China announced the mission's crew. This is not out of the ordinary, by the way; China generally doesn't reveal the identity of Shenzhou astronauts until the day before launch.

This is in keeping with the nation's broader spaceflight ethos, which prizes keeping things close to the vest.

Ali is flying as a payload specialist. The other Shenzhou-24 astronauts are commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer ​Wu Yi. Tang also flew on the Shenzhou-12 and Shenzhou-17 missions, which launched in June 2021 and October 2023, respectively. He will be the first person to visit Tiangong three times, according to the state-run Xinhua news agency. Shenzhou-24 will be the first spaceflight for Wu.

Tang and Wu are expected to live aboard Tiangong for six months, the usual Shenzhou rotation. But Ali will stay in orbit for just a week or so, coming back down to Earth with Zhang Zhiyuan and Lai Ka-ying of the Shenzhou-23 mission, which launched on May 24.

According to the South China Morning Post, the third Shenzhou-23 crewmate, Zhu Yangzhu, will stay behind when Ali leaves, living aboard Tiangong until Shenzhou-24 comes home. Zhu will therefore become the first Chinese astronaut ever to spend a year in orbit, a milestone that will allow China to prep for long-duration missions to the moon and other deep-space locales.

We're amazed at just how much is loaded into this package for such a low price. It's surprisingly good quality, too, with the unit itself being sturdy and made out of hard-wearing plastic.

This isn't a scientific star projector, of course. For that, we'd recommend the Sega Toys Homestar Classic or the Hommkiety Galaxy Projector. But even though the YunLone Galaxy Projector won't give you an accurate view of the Northern Hemisphere's night sky or a close-up of the moon, it's still a projector we recommend. If you're looking to create a relaxing atmosphere, it's one of the best star projectors we've reviewed.

The YunLone Galaxy Projector doesn't have the most attractive design: It's clearly built for functionality rather than aesthetics. If an aesthetically pleasing projector unit is what you're looking for, perhaps consider the Jiawen Galaxy Projector Light. You won't find nearly as many functions as the YunLone Galaxy Projector packs in, however.

That isn't to say that the YunLone Galaxy Projector is ugly, though. The design is basic, with a circular shape that houses a clear globe in the middle that acts as the projector. It sits on rubberized feet, so it doesn't easily slip or move around, and it's naturally tilted, so it points slightly diagonally rather than straight up. Given the wide reach of the projector, it helps spread the aurora lights across your entire room.

The projector has a solid build quality: It's plastic but feels sturdy and well-made. If you're buying for a child's bedroom, you don't need to worry about little hands being too rough when using it. Those rubber feet help prevent it from being knocked off a desk or bedside table, too.

As already mentioned, the YunLone Galaxy Projector isn't a scientific star projector. If you want to recreate actual constellations and close-ups of planets on your bedroom ceiling, this is not the projector for you. But if you're looking for beautiful, mesmerizing aurora-style patterns, it's a great choice.

Once you're connected to the app, you can control exactly what colors the projector displays. Not only can you choose from a number of preset arrangements — labeled as seasons, colors or holidays, so you can create a mood that matches the time of year or how you feel — but you can set your own entire color scheme by choosing from a color wheel. You can also set the brightness, whether the lights will have a "breathing" effect, and how fast they ripple across your ceiling.

It's a very neat touch, and it goes beyond what we'd expect to find in a star projector in this price range. If you don't want to bother with app connection, you can still set a range of colors and options from the remote control, but the options here are more limited.

The YunLone Galaxy Projector comes equipped with a laser, so it can project green laser stars onto your walls and ceiling. We didn't love the look of these, though, so it's good that you can turn them off independently of the aurora lights. You can also change the laser's brightness if you'd like the stars to appear dimmer.

Both the laser stars and the aurora projections have a very wide reach, covering most of the walls and ceiling of the bedroom we tested the unit in. Obviously, this will vary depending on the size of your room and how far away from the ceiling/wall you place the unit, but we were pleasantly surprised by the coverage offered by this projector.

The YunLone Galaxy Projector has a companion app that can be downloaded onto an Android or Apple smartphone. Once the app is set up and paired with your unit, you have full control over the colors, speed and brightness of your projections.

The pairing process isn't entirely straightforward, however, with no simple way of forcing the projector to enter pairing mode. The instructions tell you to quickly turn the unit on and off three times, but it took several attempts before we successfully put the projector into pairing mode.

Thankfully, once that's done, it should stay paired with your smartphone permanently so you won't have to repeat the process. And the app itself is very easy to use, working seamlessly to change the colors of the projection unit.

The bundled remote control (which requires two AAA batteries, not included) is a little more complex than most, offering a range of buttons to control both the built-in speaker and the light itself. We'd highly recommend opting for the app option as it gives you much better control over the unit, but if your smartphone is unavailable, you can at least set basic color and speed with the remote.

You can connect a music player to the projector via Bluetooth to play your own audio through its built-in speaker. The quality is decent rather than outstanding: It obviously doesn't match the sound of a specialist speaker, but it's as good as we'd expect any $28 speaker to be. It lacks the bass that music requires to sound "complete" but will be ideal for listening to audiobooks and podcasts.

In a neat touch, the YunLone Galaxy Projector also has eight built-in sound effects, including white noise, waves, lullabies and a storm, which some users may find relaxing and good to fall asleep to.

We have been thoroughly impressed with what the YunLone Galaxy Projector offers. Its projections are beautiful auroras that dance across your ceiling, and the ability to fully customize the color and speed is something that we really didn't expect to find at a $28 price point.

If you're on a budget and looking for a non-scientific projector to use to relax and unwind with, we really don't think you can find a better unit. If, however, you want something that offers more scientific projections, you'll need to look elsewhere.

Sega Toys' range of projectors, including the Homestar Flux and the Homestar Classic, is excellent but comes with a much bigger price tag. The Hommkiety Galaxy Projector is worth considering too, offering realistic projections but with a price tag closer to $50.

The good thing about these projectors is that they come with interchangeable discs, able to display various images of space. The Hommkiety Galaxy Projector has several discs in the box, but you'll need to buy extra discs for the Sega Toys range, so that’s an extra cost to factor in.

Kim is a Yorkshire-based freelance writer who focuses on Lego and video game-related content. She's the co-creator of GameSpew.com and ThatBrickSite.com, where you'll find most of her work. If she's not building with plastic bricks, playing a video game, or writing about doing either of those things, you should probably check she's still breathing. You can find her on Twitter at @ichangedmyname.

A spacecraft far from Earth beamed home a rare sight: a solar eclipse caused by one asteroid casting its shadow on another.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A spacecraft far from Earth beamed home a rare sight: a solar eclipse caused by one asteroid casting its shadow on another.

The image shows the Didymos double asteroid system, which consists of the larger Didymos and its moonlet, Dimorphos. In this image, Dimorphos' shadow can be seen on the surface of Didymos.

The image was captured by the European Space Agency's (ESA's) Hera probe, which was sent to rendezvous with Didymos. Once there, Hera's job is to inspect the system to study the aftermath of NASA's historic DART mission (Double Asteroid Redirect Test), which slammed a kinetic impactor into Dimorphos in September 2022 in an attempt to alter its orbit and thus the trajectory of the entire two-asteroid system.

Such missions, should they ever be needed in the future, could potentially redirect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth.

For one, this image is incredible given that it was beamed home by Hera while it approaches Didymos some 121 million miles (195 million kilometers) away from Earth.

But more than that, this image reveals incredible details of the Didymos system. Scientists call Didymos a "rubble pile" asteroid, meaning it's a loose body made up of boulders, dust, gravel and other bits of the solar system held together by the asteroid's own gravity. In the image, many of these irregular boulders and rocks can be seen strewn across Didymos and its moonlet.

Hera will reach the system on Nov. 25, and ESA will release the first full images from the mission.

#688. Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment

The depiction of the birth of the goddess Athena above the Parthenon's entrance is considered a masterpiece of ancient art. Now, a German research team has pieced together all the surviving fragments.

The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.

Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.

The Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.

The east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.

For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.

After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.

The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle."

Only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.

Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.

And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.

In 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.

Then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!"

Nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go."

The researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.

Digitally fitting the fragments together led to another important discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.

The Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.

Using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most important fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.

Alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.

There is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.

Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.

In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.

In the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.

Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.

For years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.

The exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.

This article was originally written in German.

#687. WWE Star Bronson Reed Dead at 38

WWE announced that wrestler Bronson Reed died on Nov. 27 at the age of 38 from medical complications: "He was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague.”

The wrestling company announced that wrestler Bronson Reed (real name Jermaine Haley) died on Nov. 27 at the age of 38, citing medical complications.

“Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE,” the company wrote in an Instagram tribute, “but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague.”

WWE also noted that Reed and his wife, Paige Haley, were expecting their second child together, adding, “Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jermaine's entire family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter, as well as all his friends, co-workers and fans.”

No additional details about the medical complications that led to Reed’s death were shared.

The wrestler’s final WWE appearance came at Crown Jewel on Nov. 7, when he was thrown off the stage and through tables by Oba Femi during a tag team title match, according to Sports Illustrated. Reed reportedly suffered multiple broken ribs and a lacerated kidney. He remained in a hospital in Saudi Arabia for treatment before returning home.

Born in Adelaide, Australia, Reed recalled that he’d always been interested in wrestling.

“I was always a fan of pro wrestling, since I can remember,” he shared with Sporting News in 2021. “I had my uncle who lived with us at the time, he was a huge wrestling fan, so as a little kid at 2, 3 years old, he was watching wrestling on TV and I guess I was sitting there watching as well. From there, I just became a fan."

"As a little kid, I was always like, ‘One day I’m going to be a wrestler,’ but you don’t know if that is going to happen,” he added. “As a teenager, I saw some local wrestling and that’s when I was like, maybe I can do this, join a school and learn how to do it locally."

And that certainly paid off as he won a number of awards during his tenure, as he was the NXT North American Champion in 2021, as well as the winner of the 2024 André the Giant Memorial Battle Royal.

Of course, he knew that his career was only possible thanks to his high school sweetheart Paige, whom he wed in May 2021.

“This is as much her journey as it is mine,” he shared with Sports Illustrated in 2021. “I’ve been with my wife since I was a teenager. She’s actually seen me since before I was a wrestler, when I was this huge wrestling fan and dreamed of one day getting to WWE.”

“That seems like a big dream, especially when you’re from a really small town in Australia,” he admitted. “She supported me the whole way, and it meant a lot to have her there.”

#686. How a football team rebuilt after 19 players died in plane crash

How a football team rebuilt after 19 players died in plane crash

It was 2am when Ivan Tozzo picked up his mobile phone and heard his football club's secretary screaming his name.

A plane carrying the Chapecoense team had crashed into a mountain.

Seventy-one people were dead, including 19 of 22 players from the Brazilian club who were on their way to the biggest game in their history.

It would later emerge the plane had run out of fuel and investigators would find the airline and pilot were to blame as the fuel load was insufficient for the flight on 28 November 2016.

But in the early hours, as Tozzo watched the TV news in the changing room at the club's stadium, his only thought was for the players who would not be coming back to this room.

When he sat alone in the club's boardroom after the funerals as the only director still alive, he cried.

That was the moment when Tozzo â who had changed his mind about travelling with the team because he had a sense of unease about the trip - decided he would lead Chapecoense to rise again.

Ivan Tozzo recalls the phone call he got after the crash: "It was our club secretary, Jorilda, who was desperate, screaming 'Ivan Ivan'."

Chapecoense had been travelling to Colombia to play Atletico Nacional of Medellin in the first leg of the Copa Sudamericana final, South America's second most prestigious club tournament.

It was a first continental final for the Brazilian team.

"The team was very motivated, knowing that we were engraving our names inside the history of the club," goalkeeper Jakson Follmann, one of the three surviving players, tells BBC Sport.

Aged 24 at the time, Follmann had also been looking forward to his imminent wedding, little knowing he would be spending two months in hospital instead.

"Everyone was completely proud of everything they were doing, both for the team and for the community of Chapeco and the region," Follmann says.

Commentator Rafael Henzel, who was one of six survivors of the crash but who died in 2019 following a heart attack, described the Copa Sudamericana as the team's "World Cup" and said in 2017 that "if anyone's ever died happy, it was the people on that plane".

Survivors Neto, Alan Ruschel, Follmann and Henzel (left to right) appeared together at a friendly between Brazil and Colombia two months after the crash

The LaMia 2933 flight from Santa Cruz in Bolivia to the Colombian city of Medellin had a journey distance similar to the plane's flying range, but it did not stop to refuel and crashed into a mountain just 18km from its intended destination.

The pilot, Miguel Quiroga, who was also a co-owner of the airline, died in the crash. In a leaked tape, he can be heard warning of a "total electric failure" and "lack of fuel". However, he did not make a formal distress call.

A Bolivian investigation concluded that the pilot and the airline were directly responsible for the crash, while a Colombian investigation said there was no technical failure and blamed the pilot, the airline and Bolivian regulators.

"I don't call it an accident, I say it was a crime that could have been avoided," says Follman, whose right leg had to be partially amputated to save his life.

"It's the crime of not stopping to refuel, the greed to think that he [the pilot] could get there... with the fuel practically finished."

To date, no-one has been found guilty in relation to the crash.

At the time, Bolivia did not have a system for prosecuting companies. Even when such a facility was introduced in 2021, it did not cover negligent homicide or causing an air disaster.

Charges were brought against individuals in LaMia's management - who denied wrongdoing - but in 2020 a trial was delayed by jurisdictional disputes and difficulties involving defendants who were abroad.

The plane was just 18km from its destination when it ran out of fuel

A number of key details about the disaster were established early on.

At 21:16 local time, the aircraft displayed a low fuel warning but flew on without the crew alerting local authorities.

Fourteen minutes later, the plane began its descent to Medellin airport but was put in a holding pattern.

At 21:49, the crew requested priority permission to land, vaguely citing "problems with fuel".

"I remember the lights went out suddenly; then I started praying, asking God to help us," recalled defender Neto, the last of the survivors to be found.

"But a lot of people thought the plane was just landing because it was not an abrupt fall."

Within five minutes, all the engines, drained of fuel, failed.

"Then, I couldn't hear the plane engine any more. It was just a wind. And then an alarm: beep beep beep," Neto told the BBC World Service in 2017.

Thousands of people gathered in the rain as the funeral cortege went past

Seven thousand kilometres away in the small southern Brazilian city of Chapeco, Tozzo watched the scale of the disaster unfold on TV screens at the stadium in the middle of the night.

"At five o'clock in the morning, the players' wives began to arrive. It was despair. People threw themselves on the ground and cried," says Tozzo, a local entrepreneur who was the club's vice-president at the time and had joined the club in 2009 when they were not even playing in Brazil's national football pyramid.

Two days earlier, Tozzo had suffered misgivings about the trip that were so strong that he had changed his mind about travelling to Medellin.

"It was a thing from God. It was not for me to go. I called [financial director] Decio, who organised all our trips, and I told him that I would not go," he says.

"He went crazy with me. 'Why? You agreed to go, now you do not want to go? You have to go.'

"My sister was next to me, saying, 'You need to go to this match, you worked so hard to get to this moment.' But in my head I said, 'No Ivan, I will not go', and I stayed at home."

After the crash, he had another strong feeling about his path.

"I think I had a mission here on Earth to continue Chapecoense after the accident," Tozzo says. "I was the only one of the directors left alive so I took over as [interim] president."

A sleepless week followed in which Tozzo arranged flights to Colombia for doctors, relatives and pastors to identify and recover the remains and be with the survivors.

A memorial service was organised and, in pouring rain, the coffins were brought into Chape's stadium, Arena Conda.

During the service came the news that Atletico Nacional had asked for the Copa Sudamericana trophy and winners' prize money to be awarded to Chapecoense.

Tozzo was determined Chapecoense would compete again, but none of the surviving players were in any shape to play and they only had two other squad members â who did not travel to Medellin because of injury â and a handful in the academy.

They called on Rui Costa, who had been sacked by Gremio as football director six months earlier and accepted the same role with Chapecoense, and appointed Vagner Mancini as coach.

In a matter of weeks, 22 new players were signed, most of them on loan.

Tozzo's message rang clear in the ears of the new players.

"Our fans were very sad, Chapecoense was very sad, and playing again with joy was not easy," he says.

"We explained very well the responsibility they would have."

Chapecoense's new players line up for their first match

Chapecoense's first match back â eight weeks after the crash â was a friendly against the last team the club had played, Palmeiras.

Before the game at the Arena Conda, Follmann â in a wheelchair â was joined by Neto and the other surviving player, Alan Ruschel, to receive the Copa Sudamericana trophy.

"It was the first time I had gone back to the arena, the first time I really had contact with people, because I was still hospitalised," says Follmann.

"When I received the trophy, a movie went through my head because our captain Cleber Santana should have been holding it surrounded by all of us, celebrating."

The friendly against Palmeiras was the first of 80 matches that Chapecoense played in 2017, only five of them friendlies.

There was an offer from the Brazilian Football Confederation to give the club immunity from relegation for three seasons, but Tozzo rejected it.

"How can you psych up the players to play their best if they know that their classification is guaranteed?" he asks.

As it turned out, Chapecoense stayed up on their own merits for precisely three seasons.

Chapecoense's new players faced Atletico Nacional in the South American Super Cup in 2017

In 2017, as Sudamericana champions, they once again had to face Atletico Nacional, the reigning Copa Libertadores winners, in the South American Super Cup.

It meant another flight to Medellin just months after the crash. This time Tozzo was on board.

"We went to see the exact location [of the crash]," he says. "I can't believe it was so close [to the airport]."

Chapecoense lost 6-3 on aggregate but later in the year won their state championship and finished as high as eighth in the national league in a demonstration of remarkable resilience.

The following year, in the second wave of new players, defender Bruno Pacheco was signed.

Pacheco, who has made nearly 150 appearances for the club in two spells, says: "Stepping on to the pitch at the arena was an emotional experience.

"I was representing those who are no longer with us, as well as the fans. I'm happy to be part of such an important chapter in the club's history."

After relegation from Serie A in 2019, Chapecoense won the Serie B title to earn promotion back to the top flight.

But that lasted just one season and they spent the next four terms in the second tier. They have spent this year in Serie A but will be relegated again.

Neto spoke at a ceremony in memory of the 71 passengers who died, marking the 10th anniversary of the tragedy

After the crash, Neto's only appearance for Chapecoense came as a substitute in a charity friendly in December 2017, when money was raised to support relatives of the victims.

He remained at the club as a player for two more years until being forced to retire by the pain of his crash-related injuries.

He became a Christian evangelist, and he speaks for the relatives of his former team-mates who are still seeking justice as some families pursue compensation and hold out hope for criminal convictions.

Left-back Ruschel, who suffered severe injuries and had spinal surgery, was the only player to continue his professional playing career meaningfully, returning to the game nine months after the crash and staying with Chapecoense until 2021.

He only retired this November, helping his side Juventude win promotion to Serie A in his final game, ironically to swap places with Chapecoense.

Neto presented him with a commemorative plaque at half-time in Chapecoense's game against Palmeiras at the Arena Conda on 24 November when both men held aloft a jersey bearing Follmann's name.

Ruschel referenced the plane crash in a video announcing his retirement, calling it "a day that changed my life forever".

"I lost friends, companions and people with whom I shared dreams and projects," he said.

"And God gave me a second chance. I didn't know if I would be able to play football again, but I believed that if I was here, there was still a purpose for my life.

"And today, I have the privilege of being able to choose the moment to say goodbye."

Follmann's wedding - the one he had been preparing for before the crash - did happen and he became a father.

Despite having an offer to join Brazil's sitting volleyball team at the Paralympics, he turned to careers as a singer, motivational speaker and author, but with a new perspective.

"I observe everything around me. I observe life," he says.

"I have issues with making plans for the future, because life showed me that I only have today to live.

"I don't leave anything for tomorrow. I say everything today. I forgive today, I hug today."

Tozzo, the director who stayed at home, continues to live in Chapeco where he runs various businesses.

"I haven't talked about the accident for a long time," he says. "We keep remembering, and every time we talk, tears fall, but these are things in life that we have to face."

Additional reporting by Julia Dias Carneiro

"We've caught, for the first time, a star's final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As ubiquitous as the sun is to us today, our star is not eternal; one day, albeit in billions of years, it will die. While massive stars die in supernova explosions, the sun and stars of similar mass die quieter deaths. But that doesn't mean these stars completely go out with a whimper.

New observations collected using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), the world's largest radio telescope comprised of 66 antennas in northern Chile, reveal that the sun's death throes may be different from what scientists had initially believed.

NASA Jet Propulsion Lab (JPL) researcher Raghvendra Sahai, who led the investigation, explained the shape the ALMA observations took: "It's essentially a physical snapshot of an event that, until now, we've mostly inferred from theoretical models. We've caught, for the first time, a star's final nuclear heartbeat, frozen in gas."

Sun-like stars "die" when they run out of hydrogen in their cores. This means that the fusion of hydrogen to helium ceases in the stellar core, and because this nuclear process is a star's main energy source, the star no longer has the outward push to support itself against the inward push of its own gravity.

As the star's core collapses to create a stellar remnant called a white dwarf, the outer layers where hydrogen is still fusing to form helium swell out. This expansion leads to a relatively short-lived "red giant" phase. Eventually, these outer layers will cool and disperse, leaving the central white dwarf surrounded by a so-called "planetary nebula" shell of debris.

During the red giant phase, as the stellar core is surrounded by shells of hydrogen and helium, these layers are occasionally rocked by flares in nuclear activity called thermal pulses. During these episodes, stellar material is flung into space.

To better understand this phase in stellar evolution, the team focused ALMA on a star called IRAS 06530-0213, located around 12,000 light-years away in the constellation Monoceros. This revealed a giant ring of gas that appears to be a frozen fossil of the star's last thermonuclear flare-up. This thermonuclear fossil rings an hourglass-shaped planetary nebula in the act of forming.

"Most of us think of stars as unchanging points of light, but this is a real-time snapshot of a star's death throes," Sahai said. "It's the brief, violent transition between a bloated red giant and a glowing planetary nebula, frozen mid-action."

The team was able to determine that this gas shell of IRAS 06530-0213 is around half a light-year wide and was ejected into space around 6,500 years ago. It represents the first direct evidence of the last thermal pulse before this kind of star enters the final phase of its life.

The team thinks that for around 2,000 years after the pulse, the star lost mass at a lower rate. This mass loss then increased sharply over the following 1,000 years. This led to the creation of a lumpy shell of gas now seen as a tangle of material filaments around the dying star. The fact that these filaments have a spiral shape could indicate that IRAS 06530-0213 has an unseen partner orbiting it, stirring the gas.

Meanwhile, the hourglass-shaped nebula immediately around the star began to take shape around 700 years ago, meaning that the red giant phase for IRAS 06530-0213 only ended very recently, in cosmic terms at least.

There are also unexpected elements to the ALMA observations of IRAS 06530-0213.

The team discovered an unexpected abundance of heavy versions, or isotopes, of elements like carbon, oxygen and nitrogen around IRAS 06530-0213.

This doesn't conform to models of how stars like IRAS 06530-0213 forge elements and mix them into their surroundings, though similar signatures have been seen around odd stellar objects, with violent bursts of nuclear fusion thought to be the cause.As well as seeing something unexpected, the researchers didn't detect something they expected to observe.

Dying stars like IRAS 06530-0213 have previously been known to have companions, typically sitting with them inside compact disks of dust. These disks are indirect evidence of material being dragged from the close companion star to the dying star. This is a process scientists have used to explain jet-sculpted hourglass shapes.

However, ALMA failed to detect such disk around IRAS 06530. The team suggests that this could be because a disk existed, albeit briefly, during which time it powered a short burst of high-speed jets that helped sculpt the hourglass, following this the disk simply faded away.

"Dying stars so often have hidden companions that reshape their ejected material into intricate, bipolar or multipolar forms instead of simple spheres," Sahai concluded. "IRAS 06530 shows that the story is more complicated than the tidy explanation we've been using."The team's research was published on Friday (Nov. 20) in The Astrophysical Journal.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Follow him on Twitter @sciencef1rst.

#684. 'You're not welcome here' - Chelsea fans turn on Fofana

Premier League highlights: Nottingham Forest 3-2 Chelsea

Chelsea defender Wesley Fofana was subjected to repeated boos and told "you're not welcome here" by his own fans during Friday's Premier League defeat by Nottingham Forest.

The jeers aimed at the 25-year-old were heard every time he touched the ball and came after an unauthorised interview with French YouTuber Zach Nani was released.

In that controversial two-hour conversation, Fofana also appeared to joke about missing his penalty during last month's Carabao Cup shootout defeat by Liverpool.

Manager Xabi Alonso said the French centre-back had apologised and "it won't be repeated".

But Fofana endured a difficult time in his side's trip to Forest as supporters made their feelings known.

After Chelsea went behind to a brilliant volley from Igor Jesus in the fifth minute, Fofana also conceded a penalty for the home side's second goal from Morgan Gibbs-White in the 51st minute.

He was booked for the foul on Liam Delap in the box, and then replaced by Levi Colwill in the 56th minute - just after Emmanuel Emegha had pulled a goal back for the visitors - before Gibbs-White made it 3-1 in the 72nd minute.

Emegha scored again in the 89th minute to make it 3-2, but Forest held on to secure their first win over Chelsea at the City Ground since 1997.

Alonso defended Fofana after the game and said in his post-match news conference: "We have to stick together, and everyone that is in the changing room, everyone in the team is needed.

"We need to help, and we need to go through these tough moments all together, and we don't leave anyone apart.

"We need to support everyone. That is because we need everyone, and we need the fans.

"We need all the players. We need to stick together because if not, things will get more complicated, and that's what we want to do."

Asked whether the reaction of the Chelsea fans will make it difficult to pick Fofana going forward, he added: "Well, I'm thinking right after the game, and for the next games, we will see."

Wesley Fofana has made 10 appearances for Chelsea this season

Meanwhile, Nani has moved to defend Fofana, saying the player was "clearly" not happy during the interview and admitted he had to perform better.

Fofana also explained he opted to take a penalty against Liverpool as one of the senior players on the pitch, having joined in a Â£75m move from Leicester City in 2022.

But he confessed football had reached a stage where he was "more unhappy than happy", before recovering physically and mentally.

The release of the interview has coincided with the club's poor run of form, with Chelsea losing 4-1 at home to Leeds United last weekend to make it three defeats in four matches.

The defence, in particular, has come in for criticism, with the Blues one of four clubs to have conceded more than 20 goals in the Premier League after 11 matches.

Having been subjected to racist abuse in the past, Fofana spoke about handling comments during a club-organised interview on this summer's pre-season tour of Asia.

He is understood to be one of the highest earners at Stamford Bridge.

#683. COP31: No agreement on climate science, disinformation spreading

Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's plans to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts.

But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers.

"We are extremely concerned about the situation," said a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.

The IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.

"The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this issue, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions."

At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.

That's especially relevant for the next "global stocktake," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action plans for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

The European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report covers climate protection and impact.

"It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," said a delegation source.

But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.

The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.

Disagreements over budget issues have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.

"No budget means no more IPCC," said a member from another delegation, also speaking on condition of anonymity.

It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.

Researchers with the IPCC, however, have said the timeline is attainable.

"We have no time to lose," said an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive."

But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.

In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake."

The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: At past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.

Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science."

Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks, expected this weekend.

The IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action. And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.

This was apparent in a document DW obtained that had been sent anonymously to several less wealthy countries' delegations in the run-up to COP31.

It claimed to explain the nature of Turkey's proposed goals for boosting electrification to 35% by 2035, but went on to misrepresent several core details of the plans to make them seem less appealing to developing countries than they are in reality.

At least two countries confirmed to DW that they had received the document. It did not state where it hailed from and was labeled as an "equity assessment."

The presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.

The presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.

This article was originally written in German.

'Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner.''

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Prime Video's new "Blade Runner 2099" series arrives Nov. 25, 2026, and it flips the cyberpunk universe on its head. The new show casts replicants as the dominant species on Earth, with humans relegated to second-class citizens after a global uprising.

This dreary dystopian cyberpunk realm originates from sci-fi legend Phillip K. Dick's 1968 novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," and was then so vividly brought to life in Ridley Scott’s seminal 1982 adaptation, "Blade Runner." The 2017 sequel, "Blade Runner 2049," was directed by "Arrival’s" and "Dune’s" Denis Villeneuve.

Starring Michelle Yeoh, Hunter Schafer, Matthew Needham, Dimitri Abold, and Lewis Gribben, "Blade Runner 2099" hails from creator and showrunner Silka Louisa and Alcon Entertainment founders Andrew Kosove and Broderick Johnson, who executive produce with Ridley Scott's Scott Free Productions.

Here, Yeoh's dying replicant blade runner Olwen unites with Schafer’s Cora, a human masquerading as a synthetic, to hunt down a dangerous rogue replicant that holds the key to a dark secret.

We spoke to Kosove and Johnson about being respectful keepers of "Blade Runner's" creative flame, the pitch that sold them, and dipping back into Dick's original novel.

"When the original film came out in 1982, and even when "2049" came out about a decade ago, a lot of things that these movies envisioned seemed far, far away and hard to comprehend," Kosovo tells Space. "The creation of artificial sentient beings. Today, sitting here in November of 2026, the world is catching up quicker to the world of 'Blade Runner,' with artificial technology and concerns of how do humans use this technology for our benefit without it taking over."

"Silka came in several years ago and pitched her very simple idea, which was, the next chapter of 'Blade Runner' should be what happens when the replicants overtake their creators." explains Kosovo.

"We thought that idea was going to be particularly resonant. It was simple to understand so new fans could enter the world without being steeped in the first two movies. And we thought it had logical continuity to the story canon that came before it. It checked a number of key boxes for us. Even though we talked to a number of showrunners who were much more established in their careers than Silka was at that point, she won the day with the most elegant idea in our opinion."

Johnson admits that Louisa's pitch approval was just the opening round of a multitude of responsible decisions to be ruminated over as the production process advanced.

"Once you agree that this is the story we’re telling, then it becomes a multi-year partnership in honoring all the artists and visionaries that came before as it relates to visual design and music," he notes. "Everything needs to be of the highest quality. Even though it's a TV show we feel it has theatrical level visual effects. It’s practical and tactile and analog. There’s a lot of things that come along with how you produce the show. At its core that becomes a partnership when you decide these are the characters I’m going to spend hours with and you go down that journey."

With nearly 60 years of "Blade Runner" material to play with, there’s bound to be easter eggs dropped into the tale over the course of "Blade Runner 2099's" 8-episode season.

"You’ve got Tyrell as a critical aspect of our story, but Wallace creeps into the story as well," Kosove teases. "One of the keys things was, from an architectural standpoint, things that exist in "2049" had to exist in this. You see the Wallace spires when you see the Tyrell pyramid. You have the sea wall when they're going south with the spinner.

"There’s some story easter eggs too. Silka did something really cool which has not been done in either movie. She brought in concepts that go back to Philip K. Dick's novel, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" That was really interesting. We’re really excited for people to see it and see how they respond.”

"Blade Runner 2099" arrives on Nov. 25, 2026 exclusively on Prime Video.

His work has appeared at SYFY Wire, Inverse, Collider, Bleeding Cool and elsewhere. Jeff lives in beautiful Bend, Oregon amid the ponderosa pines, classic muscle cars, a crypt of collector horror comics, and two loyal English Setters.

#681. On this day in space! Nov. 24, 1947: The US Navy launches the 1st Aerobee sounding rocket, but it didn't reach space

Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

On Nov. 24, 1947, the U.S. Navy launched the first Aerobee rocket into the sky, but it never reached space.

Aerobee was a suborbital sounding rocket designed to study Earth's atmosphere.

After World War 2, the United States started reusing erman V-2 rockets for this kind of research. When they started running out of V-2 rockets, the United States constructed its own rockets that were similar but cheaper to build and to launch. In the weeks leading up to the first Aerobee mission, three test flights were launched.

Those tests used a dummy version of Aerobee with a live booster to see if the two stages would separate properly. On Aerobee's first real flight, the rocket flew about 35 miles high. That's below the 62-mile (100 kilometers) upper limit for the boundary of space. (NASA and the U.S. military typically consider 50 miles the edge of space.) Mission control cut the flight short after about 30 seconds, because Aerobee started to yaw, and they wanted to keep it from going completely out of control.

Billed as the "most successful sounding rocket of the space age," the initial Aerobee rocket was suborbital rocket designed to launch experment payload of up to 100 pounds (45 kilograms) to an altitude of 75 miles (121 kilometers) or so.

"The Aerobee was designed to carry instruments aloft to collect data on the upper atmosphere and to place small animals in a weightless condition for physiological studies," the U.S. National Museum of the United States Air Force wrote in a mission overview. "It was launched by a solid-propellant booster engine of 18,000 pounds thrust that burned for only two and a half seconds."

While the first Aerobee rocket did not reach space, many more made successful launches in the decades that followed.

Engineers made a steady stream of upgrades to the the Aerobee rocket, allowing to fly higher and launch heavier payloads into space. It was an Aerobee rocket that launched two Phillipine monkeys on a mission to study how the effects of rapid launch acceleration might affect their bodies, an experiment that was among the frst human physiology tests that paved the way for human spaceflight.

More than 1,000 Aerobee rockets have launched since then, and the last one flew in January of 1985.

#679. NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos

"The first thing we said was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges."

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

When DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an important part of Hera's investigation.

ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify."

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit

Although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's new image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

The experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact

After a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

While DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

The findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

"Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!"

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

Materials provided by European Space Agency (ESA). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#678. Postcards from your graves

Wendy Nikel is a speculative-fiction author with a degree in elementary education, a fondness for road trips and a terrible habit of forgetting where she’s left her cup of tea. For more info, visit wendynikel.com.

You send me postcards from your graves, but by the time they reach me, you’re gone.

1) Quoted in Peculiar Letters from the Western Front, which I’d borrowed from the library the day before you left:

I’ve figured it out, B. The failsafe implanted in my wrist must have been misprogrammed. I never should have let AI help me write the code. Instead of pulling me back to the present whenever I’m in danger, for some reason, it keeps sending me into danger. (AI always has trouble with prepositions, doesn’t it?) Gotta go; they’re bombing again. Love, T.

The machine hums in the corner of the lab where you left it. “Just a quick test trip!” I keep hearing you say, your final words caught in a loop in my mind.

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

2) Delivered via Western Union, water-stained and faded, with instructions to hold for delivery until the present day:

Aloha, B. You’ll never guess where I ended up! Hawaii! A bit of a detour from “two weeks ago” (I swear, I entered it correctly! The machine must have some bugs to work out!) I’ll write again with the exact date as soon as I can find a newspaper, but it must be the early ’40s. Lots of war talk among the men stationed here. Love, T.

I plot them all out like a madman, connecting dates and places and all the catastrophes that conspire to keep us apart. I haunt disaster sites, archives and museums, searching for clues for my collection, as if completing the puzzle might bring you back.

3) Scratched onto a lifeboat oar at the Titanic museum:

Happened again, B. Not much time before the you-know-what. Wanted you to know I was here. T.

4) Sharpied discreetly on The Sphere by Fritz Koenig, displayed at Liberty Park, New York:

I hate knowing what’s coming, B. I want to warn these people. Would they even believe me if I did? T.

5) Printed in the editorial section of a 1900 newspaper:

This cryptic telegram, addressed to our editor on Sept. 8th, was the last to arrive from Galveston before the recent storm.

Please print the following in your newspaper, word for word.

“B. Trip to Hawaii was a disaster. Infamously. Zeroes got me. Somehow ended up here. Trying to figure out how to get back to you before the storm hits. Love, T.”

I am the one who’s filled our home with history, while you’ve lived your life in dogged pursuit of the future. Is it ironic, then, that you’re there, in those places I know so well, while I’m stuck here, trying to sort out what happens next?

6) From a note scribbled in the communion ledger of St Michael’s Church, Old Town, Chicago:

B — I think it’s the large language model. Like fire, it follows the path of least resistance, the most well-worn ruts in the road. What rut is more worn in the road of time-travel stories than experiencing, preventing, observing disasters? And what disasters are more well-worn than these? T.
