#585. Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry

A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations. The researchers have found direct experimental evidence that triple bonds involving heavy elements do not always behave according to the familiar rules taught in chemistry classes.

The study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy. In particular, the researchers found that two types of bonds normally treated as distinct can begin to merge, creating a structure that conventional chemistry models do not fully describe.

Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.

"This idea that relativity is important in heavy elements has been around since the 1970s," said Lai-Sheng Wang, a professor of chemistry at Brown and the study's corresponding author. "But we show direct spectroscopic evidence that what we learned in high school about chemical bonding isn't true in heavy elements."

Why Einstein's Relativity Changes Chemical Bonds

To understand why the discovery matters, it helps to look at how chemical bonds normally form.

Atoms can connect by sharing electrons, the negatively charged particles that surround their positively charged nuclei. In a simple covalent bond, each atom contributes an electron to a shared pair. The attraction between these negatively charged electrons and the two positive nuclei helps hold the atoms together.

Some atoms share multiple pairs of electrons, producing double or triple bonds. According to the standard textbook model, a triple bond consists of three separate connections: one sigma bond and two pi bonds.

The sigma bond is typically the strongest. It forms through a direct, "head-on" overlap of electron orbitals along the axis connecting the two atomic nuclei. The other two connections are pi bonds, which form through weaker, "side-by-side" overlaps on either side of that axis.

For lighter elements, this familiar description works well. However, the situation becomes more complicated farther down the periodic table.

Heavy elements contain nuclei with large numbers of protons, creating powerful electrical attractions that can accelerate nearby electrons to a substantial fraction of the speed of light. At these extreme speeds, effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity become important, changing how the electrons behave.

One particularly important effect is known as spin-orbit coupling. Electrons possess a quantum property called spin, which gives them a magnetic character often described as pointing up or down. Under ordinary conditions, spin and orbital motion can be treated as largely separate properties. But in heavy atoms, relativistic effects can link them strongly together.

That connection changes how electrons interact and disrupts the clear distinction between sigma and pi bonds that traditional chemistry relies on.

"The boundary between a sigma bond and a pi bond is now sort of smeared," Wang said. "We still have three bonds, but we don't really strictly have a sigma or a pi anymore."

Scientists Find Direct Evidence in Bismuth Bonds

To test whether this unusual bonding behavior actually occurs, Wang's research group, led by Brown Ph.D. students Deniz Kahraman and Jie Hui, created molecules containing carbon and bismuth.

Bismuth sits next to lead on the periodic table and is among the heavier elements in which relativistic effects are expected to play a major role. That made it an especially useful candidate for investigating whether the familiar rules of triple bonding begin to break down.

The researchers cooled the molecules to temperatures approaching absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. They then examined the molecules using photoelectron spectroscopy, a technique that uses laser light to eject electrons from molecules.

By measuring the energy of the released electrons, scientists can determine how tightly those electrons were held in place. This provides a detailed picture of the electronic structure responsible for chemical bonding.

The results revealed a striking departure from the conventional model.

Rather than showing the expected combination of one sigma bond and two pi bonds, the carbon-bismuth triple bonds displayed a different arrangement. Their electronic structure was more consistent with one pi bond and two hybrid sigma-pi bonds.

In other words, Einstein's relativity had changed the nature of the chemical connections, blending two traditionally distinct types of bonds into something that standard textbook descriptions do not fully capture.

A Discovery That Could Rewrite Chemistry Textbooks

The findings provide direct experimental confirmation of relativistic bonding effects that scientists have discussed for decades. Wang believes this evidence could eventually lead to changes in how chemical bonding is explained in chemistry textbooks, particularly as research involving heavy elements continues to expand.

The implications could also extend beyond fundamental chemistry.

Bismuth has attracted growing scientific interest because it may offer a less toxic alternative to lead in next-generation solar cells. Researchers are also exploring its potential in quantum materials and quantum computing, fields that depend on understanding and controlling the behavior of electrons.

A more accurate picture of how heavy atoms form chemical bonds could help scientists investigate these materials and better understand the properties that make them useful for emerging technologies.

"Maybe this will become the new textbook idea as we are dealing with more and more heavy chemistry of the heavy elements," Wang said.

The research was supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation (CHE-2403841) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-SC0008501).

Indian auteur Anurag Kashyap (“Gangs of Wasseypur”) and producer Ranjan Singh have boarded “The Melody of Destiny,” a short film rooted in the northern Indian state of Haryana, as presenters and executive producers, backing the film on the festival circuit.

The short is the first film from Chaitanya Chugh, a 24-year-old self-taught director from Pehowa, Haryana. He produced it with Diya Panjwani and Aabhar S Dev. Related Stories ‘52 Blue’ Director on How Lionel Messi Fandom Inspired World Cup Film: 'People Will Die for These Players' Candle Media’s Kevin Mayer Says ‘Urge to Merge’ Will Last Several Years as Revenue Growth Stalls

Saurabh Bansal plays Rajesh, who lives in Delhi, far from his wife and daughter in Haryana, and sings on the city’s streets in secret. He is saving for the day his daughter Priya (Miraya Sehgal), 10, gets married. She lives at home with her mother, Savitri (Nagmeet Arora). One evening, a conversation over dinner turns into a fight, and the family’s strained relationships come out into the open.

Chugh shot the film guerrilla-style on Delhi’s streets. The idea came from two moments in his own life after the COVID-19 lockdown. In 2021, his mother told him she had given a saree from her wedding to a street performer who was collecting money for his daughter’s marriage. Months later, on the way to the mountains, Chugh saw a roadside banner offering 51 wedding items for INR 51,000 ($530), and the two memories came together.

“Initially drawn from the stark reality of the importance of marriages in India, which is maligned by the illegal practice of dowry, it grew into an exploration of gendered roles and power, and how they shape family dynamics, especially in traditional setups. By looking into a household whose relationships are governed by abuse rooted in the problems of class and patriarchy, the film tries to present a documentation of these gruesome truths,” Chugh said.

Most of the crew was female. The film also draws on Haryanvi folklore, which traditionally tells stories through metaphor in song.

“The film really punches you hard at one point,” Kashyap said. “Chaitanya really knows the world that he has captured intimately in the film. It’s powerful, it’s sensitive and carries some really authentic performances. I hope the film travels far and wide.”

Singh said it is rare to see a young filmmaker try to push boundaries with a first film, adding that Chugh “does that convincingly in ‘The Melody of Destiny.’ He definitely has a unique storytelling approach and an emotional outlook which is a must for this story. I saw the film through one of the producers Diya, and strongly felt it’s a film that should be taken to the world, and thus happy to onboard the film and try and do the same.”

#582. Einstein’s 120-year-old theory may be missing something big about the Big Bang

In the earliest moments after the Big Bang, the universe was filled with an extraordinarily hot mixture of particles known as quark-gluon plasma. Temperatures reached trillions of degrees, and quarks and gluons raced through this primordial soup at nearly the speed of light. This extreme state of matter existed for only a few microseconds before quarks began combining into the more stable protons and neutrons that eventually helped form the matter around us.

Scientists can briefly recreate these conditions using powerful particle accelerators. By colliding ions at speeds approaching that of light, they produce tiny droplets of quark-gluon plasma about the size of an atomic nucleus. Each droplet survives for only tens of septillionths of a second, giving researchers an incredibly brief opportunity to investigate the substance that filled the newborn universe.

One way to explore this mysterious fluid is to observe how heavy quarks behave as they travel through it. Although these particles are not part of the surrounding plasma being studied, their movements can reveal important details about its microscopic structure. This approach builds on a principle first described by Albert Einstein in 1905.

However, Einstein's original framework has limitations under the extraordinary conditions found in quark-gluon plasma. When particles approach the speed of light, interactions occur that his theory does not fully account for.

MIT Physicists Extend Einstein's Century-Old Theory

Researchers at MIT and the University of California at Santa Barbara (UCSB) have now developed a theoretical framework that goes beyond Einstein's original description. Their work predicts how a fluid affects particles traveling at relativistic speeds, including the forces that accelerate, slow, and redirect them.

The researchers believe their calculations could help scientists better understand how heavy quarks move through quark-gluon plasma. By comparing their predictions with results from particle accelerator experiments, physicists may be able to uncover new details about the internal structure of this ancient form of matter and the conditions that prevailed shortly after the Big Bang.

"Our result reveals a new source of information carried by heavy quarks in rare, unusually large changes in their motion," says Jean Du Plessis, a graduate student in MIT's Center for Theoretical Physics, a Leinweber Institute. "How often those large changes occur depends on the microscopic nature of the plasma, raising the possibility that they could provide a new way to learn what the quark-gluon plasma is actually like inside."

Du Plessis conducted the research with Bruno Scheihing-Hitschfeld of the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at UCSB. Their findings were published in Physical Review Letters.

How Pollen in Water Inspired Einstein's Discovery

The origins of this research stretch back nearly two centuries to an observation made by botanist Robert Brown. In 1827, Brown noticed that pollen grains suspended in apparently motionless water moved unpredictably, constantly shifting and drifting despite the absence of any visible disturbance. Scientists eventually named this phenomenon "Brownian motion."

Einstein provided a scientific explanation in 1905, showing that these seemingly random movements were caused by tiny, invisible interactions between particles suspended in a fluid and the atoms and molecules surrounding them.

He demonstrated that two competing effects govern the movement of a particle through a fluid. The first is drag, which resists the particle's movement and slows it down. The second consists of countless random pushes from the surrounding atoms and molecules. Although individual microscopic particles are extremely small, their combined activity can deliver enough energy to make larger particles move unpredictably.

Einstein's theory established a relationship between these effects, allowing scientists to learn about the microscopic properties of a fluid by studying the motion of particles inside it.

Over the following decades, researchers applied this principle to many different fluids, including quark-gluon plasma. They generally expected particles traveling through such plasma to experience a balance of drag and random impacts resembling the behavior of pollen grains in water.

In conventional Brownian motion, the likelihood of different forces follows a bell-shaped curve. Moderate pushes are the most common (the highest point of the bell), while unusually strong pushes in either direction are much less likely (the tail ends of the bell). Over time, the balance of drag and random motion allows a particle to reach the same temperature as its surroundings.

But this familiar description becomes incomplete when particles move at speeds approaching that of light.

"Einstein showed that the drag and the random kicks must balance in just the right way for a particle eventually to come to the same temperature as its surroundings," Du Plessis explains. "For the types of fluids he was thinking about, he was correct. But for particles that are moving at relativistic velocities, this relationship breaks down. And we've known for 20 years that something is missing. So we have to go beyond the work that Einstein did."

Unexpected Forces Reveal Hidden Physics in Quark-Gluon Plasma

To investigate what Einstein's traditional model was missing, Du Plessis and Scheihing-Hitschfeld calculated how a heavy quark would respond to the forces inside a fluid while moving close to the speed of light.

Their calculations focused on the strong nuclear force, one of nature's fundamental forces, which governs interactions between quarks and gluons and holds them together.

The team began with a relatively simple model consisting of a gas of quarks and gluons that interacted only weakly with one another. Starting with these weaker interactions made it possible to calculate the forces acting on a heavy quark passing through the gas.

They then determined how those forces would change the quark's momentum as it moved. A stronger push produces a larger change in momentum, so the calculations allowed the researchers to predict the likelihood of impacts of different strengths.

At first, the resulting probability curve looked similar to the bell-shaped distribution associated with Einstein's theory. For small changes in momentum, the familiar pattern still held. But when the researchers examined larger changes, they discovered a striking difference.

Instead of the expected symmetrical curve, the distribution was tilted, with unequal probabilities for extreme changes in opposite directions. Powerful impacts occurred more frequently than the traditional Brownian model predicted, and unusually large slowdowns were more likely than similarly large increases in speed.

"The usual Brownian picture assumes that large kicks become exceedingly rare," Du Plessis says. "For heavy quarks, however, these rare kicks are more common than the bell curve predicts, and are not equally likely in opposite directions: A large kick that slows the quark down more than expected from drag is more likely than an equally large kick that leaves it moving faster than expected."

A Universal Pattern Could Reveal the Universe's First Fluid

The researchers next examined whether this unusual behavior depended on the particular particles making up the plasma.

They repeated their calculations using plasmas containing different types of particles and found that the same tilted distribution appeared regardless of the composition.

Even more intriguingly, they recognized the same underlying pattern in an earlier calculation involving strongly coupled plasma, where particles interact much more intensely with one another. Despite the substantial differences in microscopic behavior between the two types of plasma, the probability distributions shared the same distinctive structure.

This suggested that the researchers had identified a potentially universal feature of how fast-moving particles interact with fluids, rather than an effect confined to one particular model.

"This is the first time that this seemingly universal structure was realized and really formalized," Du Plessis says. "This gives a concrete path forward for how to better understand the quark-gluon plasma, using heavy quarks."

The discovery could offer physicists a valuable new tool for investigating the extraordinarily hot matter that dominated the universe immediately after the Big Bang. By studying the rare, extreme changes in the movement of heavy quarks, scientists may be able to learn more about the interactions occurring deep inside quark-gluon plasma.

The results also point toward an important characteristic of this primordial substance. Rather than behaving like a relatively loose collection of particles, the universe's first fluid may have been governed by much stronger interactions than a conventional Brownian motion model would indicate.

Du Plessis suggests that primordial quark-gluon plasma was likely "more strongly interacting than this Brownian motion way of modeling it would suggest. It's more like a liquid and less like a gas."

By extending a theory Einstein developed more than a century ago, the researchers have opened a promising new approach to studying one of the most extreme states of matter in nature and potentially uncovering what the universe was like during its first fleeting moments.

The research received partial support from the Office of Nuclear Physics within the U.S. Department of Energy's Office of Science, the U.S. National Science Foundation, and the Simons Foundation.

#581. Germany's Early Start Pension: Can child investment accounts help?

Germany plans to pay €10 a month into investment accounts for children to encourage long-term retirement saving. Economists say the measure may help build wealth but won't solve the country's pension funding challenge.

Germany's pension system is under growing strain as demographic change leaves a shrinking workforce funding the pensions of an increasing number of retirees.

In the 1960s, for instance, six workers contributed to the pay-as-you-go public retirement system for each pensioner. Today, that figure has fallen to just two contributors per retiree.

According to the Federal Statistical Office, Germany's fertility rate is currently 1.32 children per woman,and has remained below the 2.1 needed to maintain a stable population since the 1970s.

As a large cohort of baby boomers reaches retirement age, fewer young people are entering the workforce. Germany's working-age population is shrinking by around 1% each year due to demographic change alone, according to the German bank LBBW.

To keep up, nearly a quarter of the federal budget, over €123 billion ($135 billion), is transferred to the statutory pension system each year to help finance pension payments.

Now to help ease the pressure on the pension system, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government plans to implement a raft of reforms, including a supplementary, capital-funded savings scheme known as the Frühstartrente, or Early Start Pension.

Under the plan, the state would pay €10 per month into an investment account for every child and teenager aged six to 18.

Beneficiaries would not be able to access the money until they reach retirement age, though current plans would allow the funds to be transferred into private retirement accounts. Investment returns would be tax-free during the accumulation phase and taxed only when funds are withdrawn.

Assuming an average annual return of 7%, the €1,440 contributed by the government over 12 years would grow to around €53,000 by retirement, according to government projections.

Parents and relatives would be able to make additional contributions. If they invest an extra €50 per month, the account could grow to as much as €300,000 by retirement.

Starting to save early makes sense because of the power of compound interest, Axel Börsch-Supan, a professor of economics at the Technical University of Munich, told DW.

"But it will not solve Germany's pension problems, which stem from the pay-as-you-go system and costly policies such as the pension level guarantee and retirement at 63," he added, referring to a provision that allows workers with at least 45 years of pension contributions to retire at age 63 with a full pension.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Börsch-Supan argues that government subsidies under the program are likely to benefit higher-income families more than lower-income households.

"That's a waste of taxpayer money, because higher-income individuals are already well-positioned to provide for their own retirement and that of their children," he said.

The Ifo Institute, one of Germany's leading economic think tanks, shares a similar assessment.

It argues that the scheme effectively means "the government hands out money indiscriminately, only to reclaim it through taxes from the same citizens."

The government, however, argues that the plan gives every child a head start in the capital markets regardless of their family's financial circumstances and helps them build retirement savings and long-term wealth.

Similar capital market-based savings and investment accounts for children exist in several countries, including the United Kingdom, Israel, Canada and Singapore.

Many of these programs include government contributions, matching payments or tax incentives designed to encourage long-term saving and asset accumulation from an early age.

But Germany's plan differs slightly as it links state-funded childhood investment accounts directly to retirement provision.

The government also hopes the program will boost financial literacy among children and young adults by familiarizing them with investing, saving and capital markets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Johannes Geyer, deputy head of the department of public economics at the German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin), says there is little evidence the Early Start Pension will fundamentally change how people engage with financial markets.

"The idea is that people will develop a connection to the capital markets through their experiences with their investment portfolios," he told DW. "But this is not very convincing. We neither know what experiences the future will bring nor what conclusions people will draw from them."

Geyer stresses that the program's impact will not be visible for decades because participants cannot access the funds until retirement.

"If we start now with the 2020 and 2021 cohorts, we're talking about the 2080s. That's a bit too far in the future to be able to draw meaningful conclusions."

In the meantime, he says, the scheme's most immediate effect may be to strengthen ties between families and financial institutions, particularly if account holders make additional contributions.

Opposition parties, including the Greens and the Left Party, have criticized the plan, arguing it would reinforce social disparities and boost inequality since better-off parents could pay more into accounts.

Yet Geyer says the measure won't increase inequality per se. "Sure, wealthy families are more likely to top up their contributions more substantially. But they probably would have done that anyway," he underscored.

"A more interesting question is whether the measure can also encourage people with limited financial means to invest in stocks," he said.

Geyer points out that Germany cannot entirely escape the costs of demographic decline and an aging society.

To address the challenge, he calls for a moderate increase in pension contributions, a broader contributor base that includes groups such as the self-employed, and policies aimed at attracting more qualified workers to the labor market.

Börsch-Supan, who specializes in the economics of aging, says the government's primary goal should be to stabilize the pay-as-you-go statutory pension system.

"A transition to a fully funded pension system would actually be desirable, but it would initially place a heavy double burden on the younger generation, because they would have to save for themselves while also paying contributions for their parents," he explained.

The expert also suggests other measures like restoring the sustainability factor, which is designed to link annual pension hikes to demographic shifts, and linking the retirement age to life expectancy.

#579. JAFF Market Opens Third Edition With Call to Measure Indonesian Cinema’s Growth by Quality, Not Just Volume

JAFF Market, which organizers bill as Indonesia’s biggest film market, opened its third edition at the Jogja Expo Center in Yogyakarta with market director Linda Gozali urging the local industry to judge its growth on quality as well as scale.

The three-day market runs alongside the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF). Gozali said the first edition was conceived as an experiment. “It is actually a question that we threw into the Indonesian ecosystem whether or not we truly need a film market. And the response was definitely overwhelming,” she said. Related Stories Qatar’s Film Committee and Watermelon Pictures Forge Partnership to Co-Produce a Slate of Films From the 'Global South' Qatar's Film Committee and Streamer Shasha Forge Partnership to Co-Finance Arabic Premium Content

Gozali said the market’s third outing called for some reflection on whether the industry can “actually endure and survive the economic upheaval, the socio-political instability, as well as whatever issues that are actually evolving in the global era.”

The 2025 edition centered on local and international collaboration, she said, with the goal of turning leads into multiple deals.

“This is a transitional period, and therefore let’s define what growth is,” Gozali added. “We have to define growth not just in terms of the quantity, no. Because growth in quantity itself will reduce at a time where there are challenges around the environment. So we look at growth as well from the quality point of view.”

The exhibition floor hosts 116 exhibitors, and the opening day was reserved as a business day for accredited badge holders. Amar Bank is powering the market for the second year running.

The JAFF Future Project selection comprises 12 projects. Indonesian titles are Dhiwangkara Seta’s “Absence” (stylized “αLPα”), Timoteus Anggawan Kusno’s “Orphaned Atlas” (an Indonesia-France-Netherlands co-production), “Pupus: The Orchid of Merapi,” “A Quiet Sunshine,” “Somewhere Between” and Sidharta Tata’s “Slaughterground,” along with “Gokil,” presented with Jakarta Film Week. From elsewhere come Glenn Barit’s “Luz and Flor” (Philippines), Rein Maychaelson’s “Primal” (Indonesia, Singapore, South Korea), M. Raihan Halim’s “The Smuggler” (Singapore), Boo Junfeng’s multi-country co-production “Trinity” and Rosie Lourde’s “Wreck and Ruin” (Australia), which arrives via a partnership with the Adelaide Film Festival and Malaysia’s mylab.

The IP Connection strand, formerly known as JAFF Content Market, has opened to international properties for the first time. Of its 10 selections, four come from overseas: the comic “Disposable Dolly” (Hong Kong), the book “Cat Rental Company” (Taiwan) and two South Korean titles brought in through a partnership with Busan’s Asian Contents & Film Market (ACFM), the book “My Upstairs Neighbors” and the webtoon “Friend Request.” The six Indonesian properties are animation “Komarong,” board game “Mantra,” comics “Blood Upon the Snow,” “Lao Sam 1892” and “Yuuko’s Gloomy Days,” and novel “Hati-Hati Ada Dua Hati” (roughly, “Watch Out, There Are Two Hearts”).

Among the new initiatives is a Producers Exchange, whose first batch numbers 14 producers: Lisa Scott and Rae Choi (Australia), who come via the Adelaide Film Festival, Jason Karman (Canada, Indonesia), Nana Riskhi and Nick Musa (Indonesia), Wong Kew Soon (Malaysia), Otgontuya Zorig (Mongolia), Danzen Santos Katanyag (Philippines), Sam Chua Weishi and Wendy Lie (Singapore), Kimbo Kim (South Korea), Shao-Yi Chen (Taiwan), Phimphloi Nan Saensuk (Thailand) and Rajib Mohajan (Bangladesh, U.S.). Chua is pulling double duty: she is also one of the producers of “Primal.”

The Indonesia-France Film Lab X MTN Lab, now in its third year, is run by the French Embassy and the Institut français d’Indonésie (IFI), with Paris film school La Fémis supplying the mentors. Indonesian partners include the Ministry of Culture’s Directorate of Film, Music and Arts, whose national talent management program MTN gives the lab its name, along with the Indonesia Film Agency (BPI) and the Association of Indonesian Film Producers (Aprofi). This year’s six projects, all debut or sophomore features from director-producer pairings, are “A Straight Way to Love,” “An Interesting Incident,” “Father Figure,” “My Tears, a Sea for Jakarta to Sink,” “Saltstorm!” and “Super Neli.”

A second new program focuses on film writing across journalism, criticism and the essay form. It has 15 young participants, among them journalists, writers, lecturers, researchers and communications professionals.

The first day’s conference program includes a big-ideas session on where Indonesian cinema goes next, along with a session on how cultural phenomena can grow beyond trends and open doors to cross-border projects. The second day will turn to the question of where the country’s audience actually sits, with Gozali noting that many foreign collaborators arrive drawn by the “lucrative Indonesian market.” Sessions that day will also cover AI in microdramas, documentaries, budgets and what it takes for an Indonesian production house to last 30 years.

“Economically speaking, we are actually in a cautious mood,” Gozali said.

The final day will take in animation, box office breakouts and actors who have moved into producing, plus a talk on action and stunts from Japanese action director Tanigaki Kenji.

Ahmad Mahendra, director general of culture development, utilization and fostering at Indonesia’s Ministry of Culture, delivered a brief keynote in which he said he hoped the market would keep growing and strengthening the country’s film ecosystem, and that the ministry could lend its support. The market was then declared open as guests inserted memory sticks into a projector.

Joining Mahendra on stage were JAFF founder Garin Nugroho, festival director Ifa Isfansyah, JAFF Market executive director Ajish Dibyo, business director Sekarini Seruni, business strategist FX Iwan, board members Lorna Tee and Yulia Evina Bhara, and Amar Bank senior VP Josua Sloane. French ambassador to Indonesia Fabien Penone also attended, along with Cecep Rukendi, deputy for media creativity at the Ministry of Creative Economy, and Andhika Permata, head of Jakarta’s Tourism and Creative Economy Agency.

“People say the third is the charm,” Gozali said. “Hopefully it is, fingers crossed.”

#578. A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

The biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space. Their remaining cores collapse under gravity, forming neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. But scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Instead of exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.

New research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.

The discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, is funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and operates detectors in Louisiana and Washington. In 2015, the observatory made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, LIGO has teamed up with the Virgo observatory in Italy and the Kamioka Gravitational-wave Detector (KAGRA) in Japan. Together, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun," says LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and William H. Hurt Scholar. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin -- they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract."

Chatziioannou led the study, which was published in Physical Review D. The lead author, Isaac Legred (PhD '25), is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the work while at Caltech. Jacob Golomb (PhD '25), a former member of Chatziioannou's research group who now works at Asari AI, also contributed to the research.

Despite decades of investigation, astronomers have yet to confirm a specific case of a failed supernova. The theory, however, has a strong scientific foundation. Researchers have proposed that many merging black holes weighing approximately 10 times as much as the Sun may have originated from stars that collapsed without exploding. In these mergers, either the heavier black hole or both black holes could have formed through this process. The Caltech team set out to determine whether existing gravitational wave observations supported that possibility.

To investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA network during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample.

Even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising new questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.

"We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," Legred says. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes."

The researchers also examined how quickly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population (the spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed).

Taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions.

Gravitational Waves Offer Clues to Silent Stellar Deaths

Finding stars that disappear without exploding presents a major challenge for astronomers. Ordinary supernovae produce brilliant flashes that can be detected across enormous cosmic distances. Failed supernovae, by contrast, may leave little visible evidence of what happened, making it difficult to identify them through conventional observations.

"We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred says. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting."

By studying the gravitational waves released when black holes merge, scientists can investigate the origins of objects whose formation may have produced little or no visible explosion. The new findings provide another piece of evidence that massive stars can follow different paths at the ends of their lives, potentially revealing how a substantial fraction of the universe's black holes came into existence.

The research, titled "Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10 solar-mass peak in the merging black hole mass distribution," received funding from the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Simons Foundation. LIGO is operated by Caltech and MIT.

Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star.

That isn't a random comparison. The cannibal star, which is 350 times bigger than the sun, is nicknamed "Big Bao," while its unfortunate companion had the nickname "Little Bao." The cute cosmic monikers come from the fact that this destructive merger event has been designated AT2025abao.

A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao. This cannibalistic event was tracked by a wide array of ground- and space-based telescopes, including NASA space missions NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as well as the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. The conclusion of the event AT2025abao was marked by a massive eruption witnessed in Oct. 2025 by two instruments at Caltech's Palomar Observatory: the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Wide-field INfrared Transient ExploreR (WINTER).

"The excitement was real," team member Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "We couldn't quite believe our luck. With detailed observations for several years before the merger, for the first time, we now have an unprecedented glimpse of the conditions that lead to such cosmic events."

The story of AT2025abao began when astronomers detected a bright flash in the nearby Andromeda galaxy, a region where scientists hadn't expected to see a cosmic explosion.

Responding to this unexpected flash, Karambelkar and colleagues set about investigating its cause with a plethora of telescopes. This led to them seeing a slow and continuous brightening over the course of two years,

They determined the cause of the flash was a rare stellar merger, the luminous red nova now designated AT2025abao. They linked this to a star called WNTR23bzdiq / WTP19aalzlk that had been observed steadily brightening since 2019 after being stable for the preceding 30 years. Thus, the team determined that at the heart of the event is a red giant, a star that puffs out to hundreds of times its original size after it runs out of hydrogen in its core. The team theorizes that Big Bao, with a mass seven times greater than the sun, expanded so rapidly and violently that it swallowed its smaller companion star. The unfortunate star, Little Bao, then spiraled into Big Bao's core in fewer than 10 orbits.

"A couple of years back, we discovered a star that was gradually brightening. We took a closer look to discover a red giant, or a star that has started to expand toward the end of its life, just like our sun will one day," Karambelkar said. "Steady brightening was unusual, but even if something was stirring, no one expected to see an explosion in their lifetime, as these stars remain relatively stable for thousands of years."

An important clue to how this cataclysmic and cannibalistic event proceeded was provided by SPHEREx in July 2025, which found that before the eruption, Big Bao was fading in optical light but brightening in infrared. This indicated that Big Bao was cooling down and spewing out dense clouds of gas and dust that were enveloping the red giant star.

When Little Bao crashed into the core of Big Bao, it caused stellar material to be ejected at speeds of around 1.8 million miles per hour. This matter crashed into the envelope of gas and dust previously spewed by Big Bao, and this caused the flash of light seen on Oct. 17, 2025.

One of the final pieces of this story was provided by the JWST on Dec. 24, 2025. The powerful space telescope measured the total mass of dust and gas around Big Bao prior to the eruption since two months earlier.

This helped determine that Little Bao had a mass of around 70% of the sun's mass.

"It was kind of symbolic how the year was coming to an end as we managed to bring together the puzzle pieces from the story of Big and Little Bao," Karambelkar said. "But in my mind, this felt like a closure of just one chapter in a story that is just starting. We learned so much about AT2025abao, but we also learned much about conducting coordinated, multi-facility, multi-team astronomical discoveries."

The team's research was published on Nov. 18 in the journal Nature.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, New Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. Boglands are formed by waterlogged conditions and a lack of oxygen that slows down plant decomposition, causing organic matter to accumulate as a thick layer of peat. Peatlands occupy only 3% of the planet’s land area, but store about 30% of soil carbon. “In this liminal space, where land is water and water is land,” writes ecologist Merritt Turetsky, “a strange and haunting loveliness reveals itself.” This is not obvious to most people, who often laugh when told that she studies bogs. Such sceptics will be won over by her fascinating book.

At university, environmentalist Leah Stokes was stirred by the 2006 documentary An Inconvenient Truth, which argued that each of us is responsible for reducing global warming. Only later, as an associate professor in California, did she realize that the chief culprit is fossil-fuel infrastructure. In 2022, Stokes had a major role in pushing the US government to pass landmark legislation, the Inflation Reduction Act, with more than US$400 billion in climate investments. Her absorbing book unpacks “the blow-by-blows of how this climate law was made”.

Veteran economist James Galbraith begins his striking attack on mainstream economics in the United States by declaring that his academic discipline has long been a “fraud”. For decades, economists have embraced the idea that “power over money should be kept far from democratic politics”. And yet, oligarchs from finance, technology, pharmaceuticals and several other fields now hold political power. Economists, he argues, continue to deploy outdated tools from a century ago, which are weakening democracy.

#574. DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth

How did life emerge and survive on Earth when the planet was exposed to extreme conditions? Scientists have spent decades trying to answer this fundamental question, including how the earliest biological systems endured an environment that would have been dangerous to many living organisms today.

Researchers at Texas A&M University are now using advanced techniques that study how molecules interact with light to investigate a surprising clue about the evolution of DNA. Their findings could help explain how early genetic material survived intense ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.

The research was led by Dr. Peter Rentzepis, a professor in the university's Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, along with research assistants Keyvan Khosh Abady and Negar Karpourazar. Their study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), provides new insight into a longstanding mystery surrounding molecular evolution and the origins of life.

Why DNA's Evolution Has Puzzled Scientists

One of the major changes in the evolution of genetic systems involved the transition from RNA, which is typically a single-stranded molecule, to DNA as the primary means of storing genetic information. An important difference between the two molecules is that DNA uses a chemical building block called thymine in place of uracil, which is found in RNA.

This substitution has puzzled researchers for decades. Thymine is more susceptible to certain forms of ultraviolet (UV) damage, making its adoption seem like an evolutionary disadvantage. The problem would have been especially significant on early Earth, before a protective ozone layer developed and shielded the planet's surface from much of the Sun's harmful radiation.

Why would evolution favor a component that appeared to make genetic material more vulnerable under such harsh conditions? Rentzepis and his colleagues set out to investigate whether thymine might offer an advantage that had previously been overlooked.

To explore this possibility, the researchers exposed thymine and uracil to carefully controlled UV radiation intended to reproduce conditions on primordial Earth. They analyzed the molecules using biophotonics, a field that examines biological materials through their interactions with light. Their experiments employed several techniques, including absorption, fluorescence, and Raman spectroscopy.

DNA's Surprising Defense Against UV Damage

The results revealed an unexpected possibility. Although thymine can be vulnerable to UV radiation, it appears to favor types of molecular damage that are more readily reversed. This suggests that an important advantage of thymine may lie not in preventing damage, but in limiting its consequences and making recovery easier.

"We found that thymine tends to direct UV damage into a more reversible form, suggesting that early genetic molecules may have survived intense sunlight not by avoiding damage, but by controlling it and making it easier to self-repair," said Khosh Abady. "In that sense, thymine may have acted as a molecular sunscreen, absorbing harmful UV energy and keeping the damage confined to the genetic bases rather than allowing it to harm more vulnerable parts of the molecule."

This finding offers a possible explanation for why thymine became a fundamental component of DNA despite its apparent weakness. By concentrating UV damage in parts of the molecule where it could be more easily reversed, thymine may have helped protect the integrity of early genetic systems.

The discovery also suggests that surviving the extreme conditions of early Earth may have depended on more than simply resisting environmental threats. The ability to manage and recover from damage could have played an important role in the evolution of the molecular systems that eventually supported life.

New Possibilities for Pathogen Detection and UV Disinfection

Beyond its implications for understanding life's beginnings, the research could have practical applications in several scientific and technological fields.

The team established a new set of reference measurements describing how these molecules respond to light. These measurements could eventually help researchers identify harmful microorganisms more efficiently and assess the effectiveness of systems that use UV radiation to disinfect water and other materials.

"The distinct spectral signatures we measured could support applications in faster, more sensitive pathogen detection and in monitoring whether UV disinfection has effectively inactivated microorganisms, particularly in water-treatment systems," said Khosh Abady.

These potential applications demonstrate how investigating fundamental questions about molecular evolution can also provide tools for addressing modern challenges in health and environmental safety.

Could the Building Blocks of Life Have Come From Space?

With these findings in hand, Rentzepis and his team plan to investigate an even earlier chapter in life's history. Their next goal is to understand the forces and chemical processes that brought thymine, uracil, and other essential components of primitive genetic systems together.

A central question is whether these ingredients originated entirely on Earth or whether some arrived from beyond our planet. Meteorites may have delivered organic compounds that later became incorporated into the chemical systems from which life developed.

"We hope to explore whether life's chemical building blocks formed and assembled entirely on Earth or whether some were delivered to our planet from elsewhere by meteorites and later incorporated into early genetic systems," said Khosh Abady. "We are grateful to Texas A&M University and our research sponsors for supporting this work and enabling us to explore fundamental questions about life's origins."

By examining how DNA's molecular components respond to radiation and how those components may have first assembled, the researchers hope to uncover more of the chemical history that made life on Earth possible.

Training for a mission to space is hard work. But sometimes you have to take a minute and have a little fun with your crewmates.

Crowded together with the Orion spacecraft, the four astronauts that make up the Artemis III crew hold up three fingers, taking a brief pause in their rigorous training for some lighthearted crew bonding.

In the snapshot, the crew — from left to right, NASA astronauts Randy Bresnick (mission commander) and Frank Rubio (mission specialist), European Space Agency astronaut Luca Parmitano (mission pilot) and NASA astronaut Andre Douglas (mission specialist) — is spotted posing alongside the same Orion spacecraft that they will fly to space as part of their mission.

This brief moment of levity took place where the spacecraft currently resides at the Neil A. Armstrong Operations and Checkout Building at NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

This crew has a serious mission ahead of them. The four astronauts will launch to low-Earth orbit around Earth where they plan to practice rendezvous and docking with both Blue Origin and SpaceX's lunar landing vehicles, Blue Moon and Starship, respectively.

To prepare, the crew has to undergo months of critical training to both be physically ready while prepared to handle any situation that might come up during their mission. And while Artemis III isn't landing astronauts on the moon, it is a critical step toward that goal. If Artemis III goes to plan and NASA has a lunar landing vehicle that passes rendezvous and docking tests with the Orion spacecraft, Artemis IV might see astronauts land on the moon for the first time since the final Apollo mission in 1972.

#572. France Knights ‘Autobiography,’ ‘Tiger Stripes’ Producer Yulia Evina Bhara at JAFF Market

Indonesian producer Yulia Evina Bhara, whose credits include Venice title “Autobiography” and Cannes Critics’ Week winner “Tiger Stripes,” was named a Chevalier dans l’Ordre des Arts et des Lettres at a ceremony at JAFF Market in Yogyakarta.

Fabien Penone, France’s ambassador to Indonesia, Timor-Leste and ASEAN, presented the insignia for France’s culture minister. The ceremony doubled as the opening of the Indonesia-France Film Lab booth at the market, which runs Nov. 25–30. Related Stories James Gray on Francis Ford Coppola’s Advice That Shaped His Career: ‘Be Personal. There’s Only One of You in This World’ Candle Media’s Kevin Mayer Says ‘Urge to Merge’ Will Last Several Years as Revenue Growth Stalls

France created the order in 1957, and its cinema honorees range from Agnès Varda, François Truffaut, Martin Scorsese and Isabelle Huppert to Indonesia’s Garin Nugroho. Filmmaker Joko Anwar received it last year.

“When I read the names of the people who received this before me, I felt very small,” Bhara said. “They are writers, painters, musicians, directors, and many of them are my heroes. So when the letter came, my first thought was, maybe this is a mistake. My second was, this is not only for me, and this is true. A film producer never works alone. A producer is like a person who builds a boat, but the boat only moves when people row together.”

In his address, Penone traced Bhara’s path from Way Kanan in Sumatra’s Lampung province through seven years of producing historical theater, a craft she taught herself, before she turned to film in 2012 with a foundation that used art to revisit the past. She set up KawanKawan Media in Jakarta in 2016, with international co-production at the core of the business from day one. The company’s name is Indonesian for “friends.”

Its first feature, Yosep Anggi Noen’s “Solo, Solitude,” bowed at Locarno that year and later took the Golden Hanoman Award at the Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival. Makbul Mubarak’s “Autobiography” premiered in Venice in 2022 and went on to become Indonesia’s Oscar submission. “Tiger Stripes” won the Critics’ Week Grand Prize in 2023, and Bhara co-produced “Renoir,” which played in competition at Cannes in 2025. That same year she sat on the Critics’ Week jury.

This year she co-produced Next Step Studio Indonesia, which launched as the Critics’ Week’s new talent initiative and paired four young Indonesian filmmakers with four from across Southeast Asia. The result premiered at Cannes to a standing ovation. Bhara also heads international cooperation at the Indonesian Film Board (BPI), is active in producers’ body Aprofi and has been one of the Film Lab’s driving forces since its launch.

“Without question, you rank among the most respected producers in Indonesia,” Penone said. “Your work has helped Indonesian cinema reach new audiences and gain new recognition.”

Bhara, who said she grew up in a small village by a forest and that her family was very poor, recalled that one of the first films she ever watched was Nugroho’s “Cinta dalam Sepotong Roti,” and that nearly every film she has produced was a multi-country effort, with partners from Singapore, Malaysia, the Philippines, Japan, Taiwan, Germany, Poland, Qatar and France.

She told the room that independent cinema now faces three pressures, the first being big money and content, with young directors often told their stories are too small and too local. “I believe the opposite: the more local a story is, the more universal it can become,” Bhara said. “Second, attention. Fifteen seconds, then we swipe. But cinema is the art of staying. The third, the machine. AI can make images, the voices in a second, but a machine cannot remember what it feels like to lose someone.”

The Film Lab is run by the French Embassy and Institut Français d’Indonésie together with Indonesia’s Ministry of Culture, BPI and Aprofi, backed by French film agency CNC and Paris film school La Fémis. Six Indonesian director-producer teams were picked this year, with Éric Collin, Vincent Wang, Thibault Amti and Sébastien Chesneau among the mentors. The lab continues for the next six months.

“A first edition is an experiment. The second one is a test. A third edition tells us that something has become a habit, an institutional relationship,” said BPI chair Fauzan Zidni, whose organization joined the initiative for the first time this year. A producer who has chased international co-productions for 14 years, Zidni said he had gone to markets alone in search of partners, and pledged that BPI would keep supporting the projects after the lab ends.

Penone said most projects from earlier editions will head to Paris early next month for the Southeast Asia Film Forum’s inaugural co-production meetings, staged with CNC backing and the Centre Pompidou as partner. BPI members and filmmaker Edwin will also attend.

“Chevalier means a knight. A knight promises to protect something,” Bhara said. “So today, I promise I will keep protecting the fragile voices, the local films, the human films, and I promise I will never do it alone.”

#571. A 194-year-old tortoise has a remarkable anti-aging secret hidden in its DNA

At an estimated 194 years old, a giant tortoise named Jonathan has lived longer than any other known land animal alive today. Now, scientists studying his extraordinary lifespan have uncovered genetic clues that may explain how he has remained so resilient for nearly two centuries.

The findings suggest that Jonathan's remarkable longevity involves more than simply inheriting favorable genes. His body also appears to have avoided some of the genetic changes that normally accumulate with age, helping preserve important biological functions.

In a study published in Science Advances, researchers identified 287 distinctive genetic variants associated with protection against the effects of aging. These variants influence several essential processes, including repairing damaged DNA, limiting inflammation, controlling insulin activity, and suppressing cancer.

Jonathan is an Aldabra giant tortoise (Aldabrachelys gigantea) believed to have hatched in 1832. That means he was already alive during the lifetimes of Charles Darwin and Queen Victoria. Today, he holds the distinction of being both the oldest living giant tortoise and the oldest known living land animal.

A 194-Year-Old Tortoise With Remarkably Youthful Gene Regulation

One of the most surprising discoveries came when scientists examined Jonathan's epigenome, the system of chemical markers that helps determine which genes are switched on or off. These regulatory mechanisms typically change as animals grow older, potentially disrupting important cellular processes and contributing to age-related deterioration.

To investigate how Jonathan's biology has changed over time, the researchers compared his epigenome with those of younger giant tortoises belonging to the same species.

They found that the regulatory mechanisms associated with DNA repair and metabolism had remained remarkably stable. Despite Jonathan's advanced age, these genetic controls closely resembled those found in his much younger relatives.

The results suggest that maintaining stable gene regulation could be one of the factors helping giant tortoises withstand the biological stresses of aging for exceptionally long periods.

This research also represents the first investigation of the epigenome of a giant tortoise. The project was led by Kallel, a US nonprofit organization focused on longevity research. Its scientists believe that examining the biology of animals capable of surviving for centuries could reveal important new insights into the mechanisms of extreme longevity.

"We found that the gene regulators involved in energy production and DNA repair have remained incredibly stable in Jonathan over almost two centuries," said Dr. Justin Gerlach at Peterhouse at the University of Cambridge, who was involved in the study.

He added: "There are few creatures that could tell us more about aging than the giant tortoises of the Galapagos and Seychelles islands. Working with a really old giant tortoise is such a privilege: you get a sense of the tortoise being your collaborator, not your study subject."

Gerlach has spent several decades investigating giant tortoise ecology and conservation. However, this project marks his first examination of the biological mechanisms responsible for their exceptional lifespans.

Could Giant Tortoise DNA Reveal Secrets to Human Longevity?

The researchers hope Jonathan's genetic characteristics could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to slowing age-related decline and preventing chronic diseases in humans.

By identifying the biological systems that allow certain animals to remain healthy for extraordinarily long periods, researchers may be able to uncover protective mechanisms that could inform future medical treatments.

"Nature has already solved the puzzle of aging in remarkable ways, and Jonathan's genome provides a blueprint for cellular resilience," said Stephen Clark, MD, PhD, founder of Kallel and senior author of the study.

He added: "Our goal is to take these evolutionary insights and immediately translate them into practical, affordable treatments for everyday people. Aging is the greatest risk factor for nearly every chronic disease we face, and through the generosity of philanthropic partners, we can democratize access to longevity medicine."

Although the findings provide intriguing clues about extreme longevity, translating these discoveries into treatments for humans will require further research.

Nearly Two Centuries of Life on a Remote Atlantic Island

Jonathan has spent most of his exceptionally long life on St. Helena, a British Overseas Territory in the South Atlantic Ocean. He lives on the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the island's governor.

He arrived on St. Helena from the Seychelles 144 years ago as a gift to the governor. Jonathan was already fully grown when he reached the island, providing further evidence of his remarkable age.

The giant tortoises native to the Galapagos and Seychelles islands are among the last surviving representatives of a group of enormous reptiles that once played dominant ecological roles across many of the world's islands.

Today, these extraordinary survivors offer scientists a rare opportunity to investigate how evolution has equipped certain animals to withstand the effects of time. Jonathan's unusually stable genetic regulation provides a particularly intriguing window into the biology of aging and the possibility of extending healthy life.

#569. Southeast Asian Cinema’s Global Rise Needs Long-Term Backing to Last, Says JAFF Chief Ifa Isfansyah

The quality and international profile of Southeast Asian cinema have grown sharply, and Ifa Isfansyah, festival director of Indonesia’s Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF), wants countries to build on that by treating film as part of their cultural strategy.

He singles out the Philippines for its consistency in developing talent and keeping a presence abroad.

“I would say that, for now, it is still more of an anomaly than a fundamental structural shift,” Isfansyah tells Variety. “However, international recognition is still largely driven by the strength of individual films and filmmakers, rather than by a broader, sustained strategy to strengthen cinema as part of a country’s cultural infrastructure.” Related Stories Indian Paranormal Horror 'Numinous' Wraps, Fearfolks Takes First Look to AFM (EXCLUSIVE) British Horror 'Rise of the Rats,' Dark-Web Chess Thriller 'The Rules of the Game' Head to AFM With Black Mandala, Red Owl (EXCLUSIVE)

Isfansyah is also one of Indonesia’s leading independent producers. He founded Forka Films, formerly Fourcolours Films, in 2001, and his producing credits include Kamila Andini’s “Yuni” and “Before, Now & Then,” as well as her latest, “Four Seasons in Java,” which played Toronto’s Centerpiece program and Busan this year.

“I believe countries need to recognize cinema as an important part of their cultural strategy, not merely as an industry or a source of national prestige,” he says. “This requires long-term investment, institutional support, and a commitment to building sustainable connections with the international film community.”

JAFF’s 21st edition drew more than 1,000 submissions, from which the festival picked 254 films from 34 countries. The program runs under the theme “Influx,” opening with Lawrence Fajardo’s Filipino drama “Silenced Nights” and closing with Ueda Makoto’s Japanese comedy-drama “You Are the Film.”

Isfansyah says the current social, political and economic climate pushed the team to rethink what staging a festival should mean this year. “We did not want JAFF to become a celebration disconnected from the realities around us. This is not a moment for an excessively festive atmosphere or for pretending that everything is fine.”

Fajardo’s film, he says, speaks directly to present-day anxieties. Opening with it was meant to signal that “cinema must remain connected to the world we live in, and a festival should not be afraid to confront difficult realities.”

The closer is pitched partly at younger viewers, as a reminder of where JAFF came from. “JAFF began with a love for films like this, films that may not necessarily be grand in scale or production, but possess sincerity, imagination, and a strong cinematic voice,” Isfansyah says. “I think it is important to remember that a film does not have to be big to be powerful.”

Among the submissions, he noticed filmmakers growing bolder, especially in shorts, with more of them playing with form and blurring fiction and nonfiction. “Short films are increasingly becoming spaces for creative risk-taking,” he says, rather than mere stepping stones to features.

Many films were also more political, though not always in the sense of tackling institutions or specific events. “There is a growing urgency to tell stories that respond to the realities surrounding us.”

The “Influx” theme also nods to change across Asian cinema, from a new generation pushing against established storytelling to shifts in how films get financed and reach audiences. “However, I think it is important to look beyond the idea of change as simply a matter of technological or industrial transformation. We should also ask where these currents are taking us, whose voices are shaping the direction of Asian cinema, and what kind of future we are building together,” Isfansyah says.

On Indonesia’s local box office boom, he sees no hard line between the country’s commercial, arthouse, independent and genre directors. “Many filmmakers know one another, compete in a healthy way, exchange ideas, and often support each other’s work,” he says. Commercial hits, he adds, pull more people into cinemas, lift interest in local titles and draw investment, while challenging independent work keeps the industry diverse and credible.

Premieres matter, but they have never been JAFF’s main yardstick. What counts is whether a film merits a slot and whether it has already had a fair shot at the festival’s audience. “If we believe a film has not yet had the opportunity to reach JAFF’s viewers, we will be interested in bringing it here, regardless of whether it has already premiered elsewhere.”

As it enters its third decade, the festival wants to put back into the ecosystem that built it. This year it launched JAFF Kids, aimed at children and young audiences, and JAFF Awards, which honors individuals, institutions and initiatives in Indonesia and the wider region that have helped develop film culture. Earlier programs JAFF Community Forum and JAFF Market grew strong enough to become parallel events in their own right.

However large JAFF gets, Isfansyah says it has to keep resting on emerging talent, industry professionals and academics, and keep all of them talking to one another.

“For me, being community-driven does not mean remaining small. It means remembering that the festival exists because of the people who build it, participate in it, and give it meaning.”

#568. Rembrandt's 'The Night Watch' is more alive than you'd expect

A new project and exhibition, "The Night Watch Lives," lifts the veil on the hidden world of microbes covering one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age.

Rembrandt van Rijn's "The Night Watch" is one of the most famous paintings of the Dutch Golden Age. Amsterdam's Rijksmuseum, where the work is on display, hails the artist's 1642 masterpiece as "the turning point in his career and as the superlative example of his creative genius."

In the painting, Rembrandt made dramatic use of light and shadow to guide the viewer's eye to key figures. And unlike static group portraits typical of his era, the artist depicted Amsterdam's civic guards in mid-action, as they prepare to march out.

Beyond the sense of movement featured in "The Night Watch," the painting itself is also alive in a way that's rarely taken into consideration — through the microscopic organisms living on the canvas.

The research project "The Night Watch Lives" explores exactly that question: What kinds of life forms inhabit the surface of the famous painting?

The study is a collaborative scientific and exhibition project between the Rijksmuseum and ARTIS-Micropia — an Amsterdam museum dedicated to the world of microorganisms.

It's part of the broader "Operation Night Watch" restoration and research project described as the "biggest and most wide-ranging ever study and restoration of Rembrandt's most famous painting," started in 2019. Conservators and scientists in this project have been examining every aspect of Rembrandt's masterpiece using cutting-edge technology, seeking new insights into its materials, condition and history — and now, its microbiome.

The idea behind "The Night Watch Lives" was to "put microbes in a positive spotlight," Eline van Bloois, who led the research, told DW. "Honestly, if you're asking me — I'm a microbiologist, so I'm biased of course — but they really deserve more positive attention."

Over a period of six months, van Bloois will be taking samples once a month directly from the famous painting at the Rijksmuseum, accompanied by the people working on the restoration of "The Night Watch."

Using small sterile discs gently pressed against selected areas of the painting, the samples collect microscopic material from both varnished and unvarnished sections.

These samples are then cultivated in laboratories, allowing previously invisible microbes to grow into visible colonies that can be studied and identified.

At the "The Night Watch Lives" exhibition, visitors can view Petri dishes containing the cultivated microbial colonies. A life-size reproduction of Rembrandt's masterpiece also shows where the samples were taken, and which microorganisms were found there.

At the exhibition's opening on November 11, the installation included the findings of two of van Bloois' sampling sessions. Four more will be added over the coming months, allowing the museum's visitors to follow the results of the study as it unfolds.

That means the exhibition's visitors "will be figuring out what I've found as I'm figuring it out myself," explains the microbiologist. "We really take them through that journey with us."

People often fear microbes or associate them with disease, even though the vast majority of these microscopic organisms are actually harmless or vital to human survival.

Some of the organisms found on the painting "are very commonly found on human skin, for instance, and they're a healthy part of the microbiome; most humans actually have these bacteria with them," says van Bloois, adding that the presence of these microbes on the painting made sense, since humans are often near the work.

But another bacterium stood out in the samples: Microbacterium saccharophilum, a species first identified at a sugar refinery in Japan in 2013.  How this microorganism ended up on the Dutch "Night Watch," or when, is a guessing game.

"It's part of the fun and part of the frustration in microbiology. You cannot ask the microbes where they originate from," says van Bloois. "It would make our lives a bit easier, but it's also fun to have a little bit of a mystery."

The samples also revealed bacteria from soil, often found in plant roots. Could these organisms somehow harm the painting? Could plants start growing on the work?

Van Bloois explains why this is highly unlikely: On the painting, the bacteria can form inactive spores, but for the study, the researcher "provided them with all the nutrients and the right temperature and the right humidity that allowed them to grow again."

Still, studying these organisms may eventually contribute to understanding how paintings age, how environmental conditions affect cultural heritage, and how museums can better preserve priceless works of art.

As to whether the microorganisms could date back to Rembrandt's time, the microbiologist says that's also "highly unlikely" — but here again, microbes cannot reveal their origin story.

As part of the larger "Operation Night Watch" team, van Bloois is definitely inspired by this "group effort where everyone is just really enthusiastic about telling these stories and adding to the knowledge surrounding 'The Night Watch.'"

The microbiological samples revealed by the laboratory process resemble abstract art in miniature: colorful clusters, delicate textures and intricate patterns created by living organisms.

And as the study is unfolding publicly, it also feels like an artistic performance of its own.

The project also perfectly embodies the full name of the museum where the exhibition is held: Natura Artis Magistra, a Latin phrase that translates to "nature is the teacher of art and science," as the microbiologist points out: "It's really cool to see science and art all come together in this project."

The exhibition "The Night Watch Lives" runs at ARTIS-Micropia in Amsterdam until the end of May 2027.

#567. Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past

Ancient rocks collected from the Moon's far side are revealing new details about the violent events that shaped the early Solar System. The discoveries are challenging a scientific theory that has stood for decades and could also provide important clues about the conditions that influenced Earth's earliest history.

New research suggests that the intense asteroid bombardment experienced by the Moon did not occur primarily during a single, catastrophic period, as scientists previously believed. Instead, evidence preserved in lunar rocks indicates that the frequency of these collisions decreased gradually over billions of years.

The Moon offers a rare opportunity to investigate this distant past. While erosion, volcanic activity, and the movement of tectonic plates have destroyed much of Earth's earliest geological record, the lunar surface has retained evidence of ancient asteroid impacts dating back billions of years.

Why the Moon's Far Side Holds Important Clues

Dr. Fred Jourdan, a research co-author affiliated with Curtin University's School of Earth and Planetary Sciences and John de Laeter Centre, explained that lunar rocks preserve valuable information about the Solar System's earliest history. These natural records allow researchers to investigate events that took place soon after the planets formed.

"The Moon is like a time capsule -- it has preserved a record of events that have been erased from Earth by erosion, plate tectonics and other geological processes," Dr. Jourdan said.

"Samples collected from the Moon's far side are particularly significant because they allow us to compare two very different parts of the Moon for the first time. Until now, almost everything we knew came from the side facing Earth."

"By analyzing these ancient rocks, we can better understand when major asteroid impacts occurred and how the early Solar System evolved. The far side preserves a cleaner record of those earliest impacts because it was much less affected by later geological events than the side facing Earth.

"These samples are helping us rewrite parts of the Moon's history and suggest the early Solar System experienced a long decline in asteroid impacts rather than a single catastrophic bombardment."

Reconstructing Billions of Years of Asteroid Impacts

To investigate the Moon's bombardment history, the researchers examined tiny pieces of lunar rock for evidence of ancient collisions. Their analysis identified impact events dating from approximately 4.33 billion to 1.13 billion years ago, providing a record that spans more than three billion years.

These findings offer a new perspective on how asteroid impacts changed over time. Rather than supporting the idea of a relatively brief period of exceptionally intense bombardment, the evidence points to a much longer process in which impacts became progressively less frequent.

The implications extend beyond the Moon itself. According to Dr. Jourdan, reconstructing the history of lunar impacts can help scientists better understand the events that affected Earth during its earliest stages of development.

What Ancient Moon Rocks Reveal About Early Earth

"The Moon and Earth share a common history, but the evidence of early impacts has largely disappeared from our planet," Dr. Jourdan said.

"Because the Earth and Moon formed together, every major impact recorded on the Moon tells us something about the conditions experienced by the young Earth.

"Studying lunar rocks allows us to look back billions of years and better understand the events that shaped the environments of both worlds and helps us understand the role asteroid impacts played in planetary evolution and the conditions that may have influenced the emergence of life on Earth.

"The findings come amid a new era of lunar exploration and science, with China's Chang'e-6 mission being the first to return samples from the Moon's far side."

The return of material from the lunar far side has given scientists an unprecedented opportunity to examine a region that was previously inaccessible to direct sampling. By comparing these rocks with samples from the Moon's near side, researchers can develop a more complete picture of the impacts that shaped the lunar surface and the wider Solar System.

The research was led by the State Key Laboratory of Deep Earth Processes and Resources at the Guangzhou Institute of Geochemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The findings were published in Science Advances in a paper titled 'The bombardment history on the lunar farside revealed by 40Ar/39Ar geochronology of Chang'e-6 impact melt rocks'.
